Here is a quick summary connecting each concept in this chapter to the skill it builds.

Concept Skill It Builds Technology Safety Following rules that protect the body and information while using devices Unsafe Technology Situation Recognizing when a technology experience feels wrong Getting Help For Tech Situations Knowing the four steps for getting help right away Encouraging Safe Choices Helping others choose safety with kind words Community Values Understanding the shared beliefs behind safe, caring choices Safety Drill Practicing emergency actions before a real emergency happens Staying Safe Away From Classroom Following any adult in charge during a drill away from the teacher Health Helper Recognizing the adults whose job is to help keep people healthy and safe Locating Health Helpers Knowing where to find a health helper at school or in the community

Chapter Complete!

Great job, friend! You now know how to stay safe with technology, how community values encourage safe choices, what to do during a safety drill away from your classroom, and how to find a health helper when you need one. Healthy choices, happy you!

docs.title: Wrap-Up for Teachers
docs.text: By the end of this chapter, most Grade 2 students should be able to describe an unsafe technology situation and the four steps for getting help, explain a safety-drill strategy for staying safe away from the classroom, and name at least one health helper at school and one in the community. Keep the Unsafe Technology Situation and Getting Help For Tech Situations sections plainly sincere in classroom discussion — this is not a place for the mascot's usual light humor. The MicroSims in this chapter move from Remember-level rule recognition, to Understand-level workflow and map explorations, to Apply-level drill practice, matching the Grade 2 emphasis on comparison and cause-effect explanation. Consider pairing this chapter with a real school safety-drill walkthrough and a visit or introduction to your school nurse or counselor before moving on to Chapter 6.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This short, focused chapter addresses recognizing unwanted or inappropriate touch and practicing how to say no or exit the situation. It is intentionally kept separate from other topics so it can be taught, and revisited, as a standalone lesson on personal body safety. After completing this chapter, students will be able to identify an unwanted touch and demonstrate saying no or leaving an unsafe situation.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 2 concepts from the learning graph:

  1. Unwanted Touch
  2. Saying No Or Exiting

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Health Basics, Friendships, and Feelings

docs.title: Teacher Notes: How to Use This Chapter
docs.text:
This chapter is written for you, the teacher, to read aloud, narrate, and guide from. It is one of the most important chapters in the Grade 2 book, and it is kept deliberately short so it can be taught — and retaught — as its own standalone lesson, separate from any other topic. Please read the whole chapter before teaching it, and plan to revisit it more than once during the year.

Keep your tone plainly sincere for this entire chapter. There is no humor, no wordplay, and no catchphrase here — every word should feel calm, clear, and serious in the best sense of that word. The central message students must walk away with is simple and non-negotiable: a child's body belongs to them, they always have the right to say no or leave an uncomfortable situation, and they should always tell a trusted adult about an unwanted touch — even if someone told them to keep it secret, and even if they feel embarrassed, confused, or worried they will get in trouble. They will not get in trouble for telling.

This chapter does not include graphic descriptions of harm. It is designed to introduce and reinforce the concept in an age-appropriate way, building on body-safety ideas partly covered in earlier grades, with a deeper focus this year on the "speaking up" half of the skill.

A Chapter About Your Body and Your Voice

Hello, friend. Today's lesson is about two important ideas: knowing what an unwanted touch feels like, and knowing that you always have the right to say no or walk away. Your body belongs to you, and your voice matters.

docs.title: What Is Unwanted Touch?
docs.text:
Unwanted touch is any touch that a person does not want, that makes a person feel uncomfortable, confused, or unsafe, or that involves a private part of the body in a way that is not okay. A touch does not have to hurt to be unwanted — it can feel unwanted even if it is gentle, even if it comes from someone the child knows and likes, and even if the other person says it is a game or a secret.

It helps students to know that touches generally fall into different categories, and that the same touch can be welcome from one situation and unwanted in another:

  • A safe, wanted touch feels good and the person giving it is someone the child trusts and wants to be touched by, like a hug from a parent or a high-five from a friend.
  • An unwanted touch is any touch a person does not want — no matter who gives it, no matter how it is described, and no matter whether it hurts or not.
  • A confusing touch might not feel painful or even feel "bad" in the moment, but it still counts as unwanted if it involves private body parts, feels secretive, or makes a stomach feel funny.

The most important idea in this section is this: the child's own feeling is what matters. A student does not need to prove that a touch was wrong, explain exactly why it felt bad, or wait until they are certain. If a touch feels unwanted, it is okay — and important — to say so.

docs.title: Diagram: Safe Touch or Unwanted Touch?
docs.text:
Safe Touch or Unwanted Touch? MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: safe-or-unwanted-touch-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Remember (L1) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: identify, recognize, recall

Learning objective: Students identify everyday touch scenarios as a safe, wanted touch or an unwanted touch, using their own feelings as the guide.

Canvas layout: - Top area (100px): A scenario banner with a short, calm, non-graphic caption describing a touch scenario (no images of people in vulnerable positions; use simple, abstract, non-identifying icons such as a handshake, a hug outline, or a caution symbol) - Middle area (250px): Two large buttons: a green heart ("Safe and Wanted") and an orange stop-hand ("Unwanted -- Tell a Trusted Adult") - Bottom area (150px): Infobox showing calm feedback text after each answer

Visual elements: - Six preset, entirely non-graphic scenario captions, for example: "A high-five from a friend after a game," "A hug from a parent at bedtime that feels good," "Someone touches you in a way that feels confusing and asks you to keep it secret," "A pat on the back from a coach during practice that feels fine," "Someone touches a private part of your body and it feels wrong," "A relative tickles you even after you said stop" - Simple flat-style icons matching the mascot's visual style; no depictions of the touch itself, only calm caption text and neutral icons

Interactive controls: - Click "Safe and Wanted" or "Unwanted -- Tell a Trusted Adult" for the current scenario - Button: "Next Scenario" advances through all six cards - Button: "Reset" restarts from scenario one

Default parameters: - Scenario 1: "A high-five from a friend after a game" (correct answer: Safe and Wanted) - No answer selected yet

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show scenario 1 caption only, no answer selected Stage 2: Student clicks "Safe and Wanted" -- infobox shows "That's right. A high-five you enjoy is a safe, wanted touch." Stage 3: Student advances to the "someone touches you in a confusing way and asks you to keep it secret" scenario and clicks "Unwanted" -- infobox shows "That's right. Any touch that feels confusing, or that comes with a request to keep a secret, is a sign to tell a trusted adult right away." Stage 4: If a student clicks the other button, infobox gently and calmly explains the correct answer, always reinforcing "your own feeling matters, and telling a trusted adult is always the right choice."

Behavior: - Each scenario has exactly one correct answer; a correct click highlights the button and shows a calm explanation - An incorrect click shows a gentle correction, never a harsh sound or graphic, and always ends by reminding the student that telling a trusted adult is always okay

Instructional Rationale: This is a Remember-level objective, so the design uses simple recognition (safe/wanted vs. unwanted) with immediate, calm feedback rather than a multi-step simulation. Keeping all imagery abstract and non-graphic protects student comfort while the caption text carries the teaching content.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. No depictions of people in unsafe situations -- use neutral icons (hearts, hands, caution symbols) only. Every piece of feedback text stays plainly sincere, calm, and reassuring, since this MicroSim addresses core personal-safety content.

Your Body Belongs to You

Here is the most important idea in this whole chapter: your body belongs to you. You get to decide who touches you and how. If a touch ever feels wrong, confusing, or unwanted — even a little — you are allowed to say so.

Unwanted touch can come from someone a child does not know well, but it can also come from someone familiar — a relative, a family friend, an older student, or another trusted person. This is an uncomfortable truth, but it is an important one: familiarity does not make a touch safe. The deciding factor is never who the person is — it is always whether the touch is wanted.

One more idea deserves special attention, because it is one of the most common tactics used to keep a child silent: being asked to keep a touch a secret from a trusted adult.

Secrets About Touch Are Different

If anyone ever tells you to keep a touch secret, that itself is a warning sign. Good surprises — like a birthday gift — are shared soon and make people happy. A touch that someone insists must stay hidden is different, and it should always be told to a trusted adult, no matter who asked for the secret.

Here is a simple way to compare the two ideas students need to hold onto together.

Idea What It Means What To Do Unwanted Touch Any touch that feels wrong, confusing, or unsafe to the person receiving it Notice the feeling — it is a signal worth listening to Secret-Keeping Request Being told to hide a touch from a trusted adult Tell a trusted adult anyway, right away

docs.title: Saying No Or Exiting
docs.text:
Saying no or exiting means using words, a firm voice, or simply walking away to stop an unwanted touch or leave a situation that feels unsafe. A student does not need permission to do either of these things — they can say no, they can leave, and they can do both at the same time, even without explaining why in the moment.

There are a few simple, practiced ways to say no or exit that work in almost any situation:

  1. Use a strong, clear voice: "No," "Stop," or "I don't like that."
  2. Step or move away from the person and the situation right away.
  3. Go find a trusted adult as quickly as possible.
  4. Keep telling adults until one listens and helps — the first adult told does not always have to be the last.

That fourth step matters just as much as the first three. Occasionally a child's first attempt to tell may not be fully understood right away — perhaps the adult is busy, or does not immediately grasp what is being described. The lesson for a Grade 2 student is not to give up, but to keep telling a trusted adult, or a different trusted adult, until someone listens and helps.

docs.title: Diagram: Steps for Saying No and Getting Help
docs.text:
Steps for Saying No and Getting Help MicroSim

Type: workflow sim-id: saying-no-getting-help-workflow Library: Mermaid Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: explain, describe, summarize

Learning objective: Students explain the sequence of actions to take when facing an unwanted touch, from saying no through telling a trusted adult.

Purpose: Show the four-step process for saying no or exiting an unwanted-touch situation and getting help, as a simple, linear flowchart

Visual style: Mermaid flowchart (graph TD), four boxes connected top to bottom, plain and calm in tone -- no urgent or alarming imagery, calm color palette

Nodes (each must have a click handler opening an infobox with plain, sincere definition text): 1. "This Touch Feels Wrong" (start node) -- click shows "This is the moment you notice a touch that feels unwanted, confusing, or unsafe. Trust that feeling." 2. "Say No or Move Away" -- click shows "Use a strong voice to say no, or simply step away. You do not need permission to do either." 3. "Go Find a Trusted Adult" -- click shows "Walk to a parent, guardian, teacher, or school counselor as soon as you can." 4. "Keep Telling Until Someone Helps" -- click shows "Tell exactly what happened. If the first adult does not understand or help, tell another trusted adult. You will never be in trouble for telling."

Connections: Straight top-to-bottom arrows connecting node 1 to node 2, node 2 to node 3, and node 3 to node 4 -- no branches, since the same steps apply every time

Color coding: Calm blue-gray tones throughout; no red or alarming colors, matching the plainly sincere tone required for this content

Interactive features: click directive on every node in the Mermaid syntax, mapped to a JavaScript function that opens an infobox with the definition text above

Implementation: Mermaid flowchart with click bindings; render inside a small wrapper page that displays the infobox below the diagram. Keep the visual plain, calm, and reassuring throughout.

A student practicing "saying no or exiting" should know that it can look different depending on the moment — sometimes it is a loud, firm "No!," sometimes it is quietly getting up and leaving the room, and sometimes it is both at once. There is no single "right" way to do it, as long as it gets the child away from the unwanted touch and toward a trusted adult.

It Is Okay If It Feels Hard

Saying no to someone you know, or walking away from a grown-up, can feel hard — even scary. That's okay. It is still the right thing to do, and telling afterward is just as important as saying no in the moment.

The single most important message of this entire chapter is what happens after saying no or exiting: telling a trusted adult. A student should never be made to feel that they have failed if they were not able to say no in the moment, or if the touch already happened before they could get away. Telling a trusted adult afterward is just as important, and always available, no matter how much time has passed.

You Will Never Be in Trouble for Telling

No matter what happened, no matter what anyone told you to say or not say, and no matter how much time has passed — telling a trusted adult about an unwanted touch is always the right choice, and you will never be in trouble for doing it.

Here is a quick summary connecting both concepts in this chapter to the skill each one builds.

Concept What It Means Skill It Builds Unwanted Touch Any touch that feels wrong, confusing, or unsafe to the person receiving it Recognizing and trusting one's own feelings about touch Saying No Or Exiting Using words or movement to stop or leave an unwanted-touch situation, then telling a trusted adult Acting on that feeling and getting help right away

You Know What To Do

You did important learning today, friend. You know that your body belongs to you, that you can say no or walk away from an unwanted touch, and that telling a trusted adult is always the right choice — every single time.

docs.title: Wrap-Up for Teachers
docs.text: By the end of this chapter, most Grade 2 students should be able to describe what makes a touch feel unwanted and demonstrate at least one way to say no or exit such a situation, followed by telling a trusted adult. Because this is core child-abuse-prevention content, plan to revisit this lesson more than once during the year rather than teaching it only a single time. Reinforce the three anchor messages in every retelling: a child's body belongs to them, they always have the right to say no or leave, and they should always tell a trusted adult — even if told to keep a secret, and even if they worry about getting in trouble. Consider pairing this chapter with your school counselor or school-based prevention curriculum, and make sure students know, by name, at least one trusted adult at school they can go to if a parent or guardian is not available.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This capstone chapter examines how family, school, and media or technology influence health practices and behaviors, and revisits active listening as a communication skill. Students learn to describe options and potential outcomes for a health-related decision, then apply goal-setting by determining actions that support a personal health goal and reflecting on their progress. The chapter closes with modeling positive health choices for others. After completing this chapter, students will be able to identify an influence on their health behavior, weigh a decision's outcomes, and set and reflect on a personal health goal.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 10 concepts from the learning graph:

  1. Influence
  2. Family And School Influence
  3. Media Influence
  4. Active Listening
  5. Health Decision Options
  6. Decision Outcomes
  7. Goal Setting
  8. Goal-Supporting Actions
  9. Reflecting On Goal Progress
  10. Modeling Positive Health Choices

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Health Basics, Friendships, and Feelings
  • Chapter 5: Technology, Community, and Emergency Safety

docs.title: Teacher Notes: How to Use This Chapter
docs.text:
This is the final chapter of the Grade 2 book, and it works differently than the chapters before it. Instead of a single safety or wellness topic, it steps back and asks: where do health habits come from, and how does a person get better at choosing and reaching them? The chapter moves through three connected skills — noticing an influence, weighing a decision, and setting a goal — before landing on the idea that a Grade 2 student can also be a positive influence for someone else.

As with every chapter in this book, the text below is written for you, the teacher, to read, adapt, and narrate aloud. The interactive MicroSims are the place where students do their own thinking and clicking.

One More Adventure Together

Hello again, friend! Today we look at where our health choices come from, how to think through a decision, and how to set a goal and stick with it. Healthy choices, happy you!

docs.title: What Is an Influence?
docs.text:
An influence is anything that shapes the choices a person makes or the way a person acts, without necessarily making the choice for them. Influences are everywhere, and most days a student experiences dozens of them without noticing: a parent packing a lunch, a rule posted in the school hallway, a jingle heard during a cartoon, a friend suggesting a game at recess. None of these things force a choice, but each one nudges it.

It helps students to sort influences into a few familiar sources:

  • People close to a student, such as family members, teachers, and friends
  • Places a student spends time, such as home, school, and community spaces
  • Messages a student sees or hears, such as advertisements, shows, apps, and packaging

Recognizing an influence is the first step toward deciding whether to follow it. Not every influence points toward a healthy choice, and a student does not have to follow an influence just because it is there. Naming the influence out loud — "That commercial is trying to get me to want sugary cereal" — is itself a useful health skill.

docs.title: Diagram: Where Does This Idea Come From?
docs.text:
Where Does This Idea Come From? MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: where-does-this-idea-come-from-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Remember (L1) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: identify, recognize, sort

Learning objective: Students identify everyday examples as being influenced mainly by family, school, or media/technology.

Canvas layout: - Top area (100px): A card showing one short example phrase, such as "Dad makes sure everyone eats vegetables at dinner" - Middle area (250px): Three labeled drop zones or buttons side by side: "Family," "School," "Media/Technology" - Bottom area (150px): Infobox with feedback text

Visual elements: - Eight preset example cards: "Dad makes sure everyone eats vegetables at dinner," "The school has a rule about washing hands before lunch," "A video ad shows a toy that promises to make you happy," "Grandma teaches a family recipe that is passed down every year," "The gym teacher explains why stretching matters," "A cartoon character says a snack brand is 'the best,'" "A big sibling models wearing a helmet while biking," "An app sends a reminder to drink water" - Simple flat icons for each zone: a house (Family), a school building (School), a screen/megaphone (Media/Technology)

Interactive controls: - Click a card, then click the matching zone - Button: "Next Example" - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - Example 1: "Dad makes sure everyone eats vegetables at dinner" (correct answer: Family) - No zone selected yet

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show example 1 text only Stage 2: Student clicks "Family" -- infobox shows "Yes! Family members often shape the foods we eat and the habits we practice at home." Stage 3: Student advances to the ad example and clicks "Media/Technology" -- infobox shows "Right. Ads and shows try to influence what we want, even when they don't say so directly." Stage 4: If a student picks the wrong zone, infobox gently explains which source fits best and why

Behavior: - Each example has one best-fit answer; correct clicks highlight the zone and show a short explanation - Incorrect clicks show a calm correction that names the correct source

Instructional Rationale: This is a Remember-level objective focused on recognizing categories of influence, so a simple three-bin sorting task with immediate feedback is appropriate; no multi-step simulation is needed.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep icons simple and flat, matching the mascot's visual style. Rotate through all eight examples before repeating.

docs.title: Family and School Influence
docs.text:
Family and school influence describes the specific ways that a student's household and school shape health practices — through routines, rules, modeling, and direct teaching. A family might set a bedtime, choose the food available at home, or show through everyday habits (like buckling a seatbelt without being asked) what healthy behavior looks like. A school might set a handwashing routine, offer recess and physical education, or post rules about kindness and safety.

Family and school influences often work by repetition and modeling rather than a single lecture. A student who sees an adult wash their hands before every meal is likely to absorb that habit even without being told "always do this." This is one reason adults are encouraged to model the behaviors they want children to adopt — a theme this chapter returns to at the very end.

docs.title: Media Influence
docs.text:
Media influence is the way that television, video, apps, games, packaging, and advertising shape what a student believes, wants, or does — often by being entertaining, repeating a message many times, or using bright colors and catchy music. Unlike a family rule or a school policy, media messages are usually created by companies trying to sell a product, so they do not always point toward the healthiest choice.

A student does not need to be able to name every advertising technique to build this skill. It is enough to practice a simple pause-and-question habit:

  1. Notice the message ("This show says this cereal will make me a superhero").
  2. Ask who made the message and why ("A company wants me to buy their cereal").
  3. Decide separately whether the choice is actually healthy, using what they already know about food, safety, or activity.

docs.title: Diagram: Family, School, and Media Influence Map
docs.text:
Family, School, and Media Influence Map

Type: graph-model sim-id: influence-sources-graph Library: vis-network Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: explain, compare, classify

Learning objective: Students explain how family, school, and media each influence health practices and behaviors, and compare how each source sends its message.

Node types: 1. Center node "My Health Choices" (large gold circle) 2. Source nodes (three medium circles): "Family" (green), "School" (blue), "Media/Technology" (orange) 3. Example nodes (small squares, several per source): under Family -- "Bedtime routine," "Meals at home"; under School -- "Handwashing rule," "Recess time"; under Media -- "Cereal commercial," "App reminder"

Edge types: 1. SHAPES (arrow from each source node to "My Health Choices") -- hover shows "This source influences health choices through everyday routines and messages" 2. EXAMPLE_OF (line from each example node to its source node) -- hover shows a one-sentence description of that specific example

Layout: Hierarchical, with "My Health Choices" in the center and the three sources arranged around it, examples branching outward from each source

Interactive features: - Hover any node: show its short definition in a side panel - Click a source node: highlight only that source and its examples, dim the rest - Click an example node: infobox explains how that example influences behavior - Zoom with mouse wheel, pan by dragging background

Visual styling: - Family = green, School = blue, Media/Technology = orange, matching the color key used elsewhere in this chapter - Center node larger than source nodes; source nodes larger than example nodes

Legend: Color key explaining Family/School/Media colors and an icon key for the two edge types

Implementation: vis-network JavaScript library, canvas size responsive, default 700x450px

A Simple Question to Ask

Next time you see an ad, try asking: "Who made this, and what do they want me to do?" That question alone helps you think instead of just reacting.

Here is a quick comparison of the three influence sources covered so far.

Influence Source How It Sends Its Message Example Family Everyday routines, rules, and modeling at home A parent packs a piece of fruit in every lunch School Classroom rules, teaching, and daily schedule A teacher leads a handwashing routine before snack Media/Technology Ads, shows, apps, and packaging, often trying to sell something A commercial says a sugary drink will make you happy

docs.title: Active Listening
docs.text:
Active listening is paying close, respectful attention to a speaker — with eyes, ears, and body — and responding in a way that shows the message was understood. Grade 2 students met active listening in an earlier chapter as a way to support a friend's feelings; here it returns as a tool for understanding influences and decisions, especially when a family member, teacher, or trusted adult is explaining a rule or offering advice.

Active listening in Grade 2 has a few simple, practiced parts:

  • Facing the speaker and giving quiet attention
  • Waiting for a pause instead of interrupting
  • Nodding or giving a small verbal cue ("okay," "I see") to show understanding
  • Asking a short question if something is unclear, such as "Why do we do it that way?"

When a trusted adult explains a health rule, active listening helps a student understand not just what to do, but why it matters — and that "why" makes the rule easier to remember and follow later, on their own.

docs.title: Diagram: Are You Listening Actively?
docs.text:
Are You Listening Actively? MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: active-listening-checklist-microsim Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: demonstrate, practice, use

Learning objective: Students apply active listening behaviors by selecting which actions in a short scenario show active listening.

Canvas layout: - Top area (120px): Short scenario text, e.g., "A teacher explains a new hallway safety rule." - Middle area (260px): Four action cards students can mark as "Active Listening" or "Not Active Listening": "Looking at the teacher and staying quiet," "Waving hands and talking to a friend," "Asking 'why do we do it this way?' after the teacher finishes," "Nodding to show understanding" - Bottom area (120px): Infobox with feedback and running score

Interactive controls: - Click each action card to mark it - Button: "Check My Answers" - Button: "New Scenario" (cycles through 3 total scenarios) - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - Scenario 1 active; no cards marked yet

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show scenario and four unmarked action cards Stage 2: Student marks cards, clicks "Check My Answers" -- correct cards turn green, incorrect turn orange Stage 3: Infobox explains each answer: "Looking and staying quiet shows active listening because it shows attention," "Talking to a friend is not active listening because attention is elsewhere" Stage 4: Student clicks "New Scenario" to try a fresh set of four actions

Behavior: - Score tracks correct identifications across all three scenarios - Feedback always names the specific active-listening behavior involved

Instructional Rationale: This is an Apply-level objective, so the design asks students to apply the concept to new scenario actions rather than simply recall a definition, matching the "demonstrate active listening in a variety of situations" benchmark.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep scenarios varied (home, classroom, playground) so the skill transfers across settings.

docs.title: Health Decision Options and Decision Outcomes
docs.text:
Once a student notices an influence, the next skill is making a decision about it. Health decision options are the different choices available to a person facing a health-related situation — usually there is more than one reasonable path, not just one right answer and one wrong answer. Decision outcomes are the results, good or less good, that follow from each option — including how the choice affects the student's own body, feelings, and the people around them.

Consider a simple, familiar example: a student is offered a sugary drink at a birthday party.

  • Option 1: Drink the sugary drink. Possible outcome: it tastes exciting in the moment, but too much sugar can lead to a stomachache or an energy crash later.
  • Option 2: Ask for water or milk instead. Possible outcome: less exciting in the moment, but the body feels steadier afterward.
  • Option 3: Have a small amount of the sugary drink and also drink water. Possible outcome: a balance that lets the student enjoy the party while limiting how much sugar they take in.

There is rarely only one "correct" option — the skill is learning to name the options and think ahead about what each one might lead to, rather than picking automatically.

Think Ahead Before You Choose

Before you decide, try asking yourself: "What are my choices here, and what might happen after each one?" That short pause is the whole skill.

docs.title: Diagram: Decision Options and Outcomes Explorer
docs.text:
Decision Options and Outcomes Explorer MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: decision-options-outcomes-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: describe, explain, compare

Learning objective: Students describe two or more options for a health-related decision and the likely outcome of each option.

Canvas layout: - Top area (100px): A health-related scenario prompt selectable from a dropdown (e.g., "You are offered a sugary drink at a party," "A friend wants you to skip washing hands before snack," "You are choosing how to spend recess time") - Middle area (280px): Two or three option cards displayed side by side, each with a "Show Outcome" button beneath it - Bottom area (120px): Outcome panel showing the result text for the most recently clicked option

Interactive controls: - Dropdown: Select scenario (3 total) - Button under each option card: "Show Outcome" - Button: "Compare All Outcomes" (reveals all outcome text at once, side by side) - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - Scenario: "You are offered a sugary drink at a party" - Options shown: "Drink it," "Ask for water instead," "Have a little of both" - No outcome revealed yet

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show scenario and unopened option cards, no outcomes visible Stage 2: Student clicks "Show Outcome" under "Drink it" -- panel shows "Tastes exciting now, but a lot of sugar can lead to a stomachache or low energy later." Stage 3: Student clicks "Show Outcome" under "Ask for water instead" -- panel shows "Less exciting in the moment, but your body feels steady afterward." Stage 4: Student clicks "Compare All Outcomes" -- all outcome texts appear together so the student can weigh them side by side

Behavior: - Every option always has a described outcome, calm and non-judgmental in tone -- no option is framed as "bad," only as leading to a different result - Switching scenarios resets revealed outcomes

Instructional Rationale: This is an Understand-level objective ("describe options and potential outcomes"), so the design emphasizes step-through data visibility of concrete outcome text for each option rather than animation, letting students compare real outcome language side by side.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep all outcome language balanced and non-judgmental; avoid depicting any option as shameful.

There Isn't Just One Right Answer

Weighing options can feel tricky at first, and that's okay. You're not looking for a trick question — you're just practicing thinking ahead. That gets easier every time you try it.

docs.title: Goal Setting
docs.text:
Goal setting is choosing a specific, personal health target that a student wants to work toward, such as drinking more water, trying one new vegetable each week, or getting outside to play every day after school. A good Grade 2 goal is small enough to reach in a short time and clear enough that the student can tell whether they reached it.

A simple goal has a few parts a Grade 2 student can name:

  • What the goal is (drink water instead of soda most days)
  • How long the goal lasts (this week, or for the next two weeks)
  • How the student will know they reached it (counting the days, or a sticker on a calendar)

docs.title: Diagram: Build a Health Goal
docs.text:
Build a Health Goal MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: build-a-health-goal-microsim Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: determine, organize, construct

Learning objective: Students determine the components of a personal health-related goal by assembling a goal from a target behavior, a time frame, and a way to track progress.

Canvas layout: - Left side (350px): Three selection columns: "Pick a Target" (e.g., drink water, try a new food, play outside, sleep on time), "Pick a Time Frame" (this week, two weeks, this month), "Pick a Tracker" (calendar stickers, tally marks, checklist) - Right side (250px): A built "My Goal" card that assembles the three chosen pieces into one readable sentence

Visual elements: - Three vertical lists of clickable option chips - A goal card that updates live as choices are made, styled like a simple certificate

Interactive controls: - Click one chip from each of the three columns - Button: "Build My Goal" (finalizes the sentence on the card) - Button: "Start Over"

Default parameters: - No chips selected; goal card shows placeholder text "Pick a target, a time frame, and a tracker to build your goal"

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show three empty columns and placeholder goal card Stage 2: Student picks "drink water" -- goal card updates to show "My goal: drink water " Stage 3: Student picks "this week" -- goal card updates to "My goal: drink water this week " Stage 4: Student picks "calendar stickers" -- goal card completes: "My goal: drink water this week, and I'll track it with calendar stickers"

Behavior: - Goal card always reflects current selections live - "Build My Goal" locks in the sentence and shows a small celebration highlight (color flash, not sound) on the card

Instructional Rationale: This is an Analyze-level objective ("determine actions that support a personal health-related goal"), so the design has students organize the separate components (target, time frame, tracker) into a coherent structure themselves rather than simply recalling a premade goal.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep the interface simple with large clickable chips appropriate for early-elementary fine motor skills.

A goal doesn't have to be big to matter — drinking one more glass of water a day or trying one new vegetable this week both count as real, worthwhile health goals.

docs.title: Goal-Supporting Actions
docs.text:
Goal-supporting actions are the specific, repeatable steps a student takes that move them toward their goal. Setting a goal names the destination; goal-supporting actions are the everyday steps that get a student there. For a goal like "drink water instead of soda this week," supporting actions might include:

  1. Filling a water bottle each morning
  2. Asking for water at meals instead of soda
  3. Keeping a small chart to mark each successful day

Without supporting actions, a goal stays a wish. With them, it becomes a plan.

docs.title: Reflecting on Goal Progress
docs.text:
Reflecting on goal progress means looking back, after some time has passed, at how the goal-supporting actions actually went — what worked, what was hard, and what the student might try differently next time. Reflection is not about grading the goal as a pure success or failure; it is about noticing patterns and adjusting.

A student reflecting on a goal might ask:

  • Did I do the supporting actions most days, or only sometimes?
  • What made it easy on the days it worked?
  • What got in the way on the days it didn't?
  • Do I want to keep the same goal, adjust it, or try something new?

This connects directly to an earlier Grade 2 skill: recognizing how current practices and behaviors make you feel. Part of good reflection is simply noticing feelings — proud, tired, disappointed, motivated — and treating those feelings as useful information rather than something to ignore.

docs.title: Diagram: My Goal Progress Tracker
docs.text:
My Goal Progress Tracker

Type: chart sim-id: goal-progress-tracker-chart Library: Chart.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Evaluate (L5) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: assess, judge, reflect

Learning objective: Students reflect on the results of working toward a personal health-related goal by reviewing a week of sample progress data and judging what went well and what to change.

Chart type: Bar chart with a toggle to a simple weekly calendar view

Purpose: Show a sample week of goal-tracking data ("Drink water instead of soda") so students can practice reflecting on progress rather than only setting goals

X-axis: Day of the week (Mon-Sun) Y-axis: Goal met? (Yes = full bar height, No = short bar height)

Data series: - Sample week: Mon (Yes), Tue (Yes), Wed (No), Thu (Yes), Fri (No), Sat (Yes), Sun (Yes)

Interactive features (REQUIRED): - Hover any bar to see a tooltip with that day's result and a short reflection prompt, e.g., hovering Wednesday shows "No -- what might have made this day harder? A busy afternoon? Forgetting the water bottle?" - Click "Toggle My Own Week" button to let a student (via teacher-led class discussion) click each day to mark Yes/No and generate their own bar chart live - Button: "Show Reflection Questions" reveals three prompts below the chart: "Which days were easiest? Which were hardest? What is one thing to try next week?"

Title: "My Goal Progress: Drink Water Instead of Soda" Legend: Green bars = goal met, gray bars = not met that day

Color scheme: Green for "Yes," soft gray for "No" -- non-judgmental, no red or negative coloring

Annotations: Small star icon over the day with the longest streak

Implementation: Chart.js bar chart with custom click handling to let a class build its own sample week interactively

Looking Back Helps You Move Forward

You don't need a perfect week to make progress. Looking back at what worked — and what didn't — is how a goal turns into a habit.

docs.title: Modeling Positive Health Choices
docs.text:
The chapter's final concept brings everything full circle. Modeling positive health choices means showing healthy behavior through one's own actions so that other people — younger students, classmates, or family members — see it and are influenced by it, the same way this chapter opened with family and school influencing a Grade 2 student. A student who chooses water at lunch, speaks kindly during a disagreement, or wears a helmet while biking is not just making a private choice — they are quietly becoming an influence for someone else, just like the influences described at the start of this chapter.

This idea connects three concepts from this chapter into one loop:

Concept Direction of Influence Example Family and School Influence Adults and school shape the student A teacher models washing hands before snack Media Influence Messages shape the student An ad models buying a certain drink Modeling Positive Health Choices The student shapes others A student models drinking water, and a friend tries it too

A student does not need a title or a special role to model a positive health choice — younger siblings, classmates, and even adults often notice and copy the everyday choices of the people around them.

docs.title: Diagram: Be the Influence
docs.text:
Be the Influence MicroSim

Type: workflow sim-id: be-the-influence-workflow Library: Mermaid Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: demonstrate, model, apply

Learning objective: Students demonstrate understanding of how a personal healthy choice can model positive health behavior for others.

Purpose: Show a simple cycle -- a student makes a healthy choice, someone notices, and that person is influenced to try it too -- reinforcing that influence flows in both directions

Visual style: Mermaid flowchart (graph LR) arranged as a loop with four boxes

Nodes (each must have a click handler opening an infobox with plain definition/example text): 1. "I Make a Healthy Choice" -- click shows example: "I choose water instead of soda at lunch." 2. "Someone Notices" -- click shows: "A friend or younger sibling sees what I chose." 3. "They Try It Too" -- click shows: "They decide to try the same healthy choice." 4. "Now They Might Model It For Someone Else" -- click shows: "The healthy choice keeps spreading to new people, the same way family, school, and media influence us."

Connections: Arrows connecting node 1 to node 2 to node 3 to node 4, and a return arrow from node 4 back to node 1 to show the cycle can repeat with a new person

Color coding: Warm gold and green tones to convey a positive, encouraging cycle

Interactive features: click directive on every node in Mermaid syntax, each mapped to an infobox with the example text above

Implementation: Mermaid flowchart with click bindings, rendered with an infobox panel beneath the diagram

You Finished the Grade 2 Book!

Look how far you've come, friend! This year you explored health, friendships, and feelings, learned about food, worked through conflicts, protected your body from environmental risks, stayed safe with technology and in your community, spoke up about body safety, and now you know how influences, decisions, and goals fit together. Healthy choices, happy you — see you in Grade 3!

docs.title: Wrap-Up for Teachers
docs.text: By the end of this chapter, most Grade 2 students should be able to name an influence on a health behavior, sort influences by source (family, school, media/technology), describe at least two options and likely outcomes for a simple health decision, and explain the basic parts of a personal health goal (a target, a time frame, and a way to track it), along with the idea of reflecting on how it went. The "modeling positive health choices" concept works well as a closing classroom discussion: ask students to name one healthy choice they could model for a younger student or sibling this week, and revisit it briefly the following week as an informal reflection exercise, tying together the goal-setting and reflection skills taught in this chapter.

docs.title: Learning Graph — Grade 2
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for the Grade 2 band of the Health Education intelligent textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this band. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the band. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

This band's graph is intentionally smaller than a general-purpose graph — 55 concepts rather than 200 — because Grade 2 health benchmarks are identify/describe-level content, with emerging comparison and simple cause-effect reasoning, for 7-8 year olds (see the Course Description Assessment for the rationale). It builds directly on the Kindergarten (45-concept) and Grade 1 (55-concept) bands' graphs and uses the same 7-category taxonomy for cross-band comparability.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this band. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Grade 2 course description is a well-structured, standards-traceable document derived from the 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards. It enumerates 25 benchmark-coded topics across five content strands (Food and Nutrition, Human Growth and Development, Mental and Emotional Health, Personal Health and Wellness, Personal Safety and Violence Prevention) plus a cross-cutting Skill Standards group, and organizes learning outcomes using the 2001 Bloom's Taxonomy (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, with a first small foothold into Evaluate — and Create still deliberately thin/absent per the developmental design of the K-12 standards, explicitly documented in the text rather than an oversight).

Because this is a Grade 2 (early elementary, independent-reading) band, the topic set is intentionally narrow — identify/describe-level content plus emerging comparison and simple cause-effect reasoning, rather than multi-step analysis or design tasks. This assessment therefore evaluates the description against a right-sized concept target of approximately 50-55 concepts, not the skill's generic 200-concept default, which would force invented content not grounded in the standards.

docs.title: Strengths
docs.text:
• Every topic traces to a specific MDE benchmark code, giving the learning graph strong provenance.

  • Clear five-strand + Skill Standards structure maps cleanly onto the same taxonomy scheme used for Kindergarten and Grade 1, supporting cross-band comparability.

  • Key Vocabulary section (17 terms) gives ready-made concept candidates.

  • Explicit "Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band" section clarifies which K-1 ideas are assumed but not re-taught.

  • First appearance of an Evaluate-level outcome (reflecting on goal progress) shows a documented, deliberate developmental progression rather than an abrupt jump, and the Analyze level now includes a genuine comparison task (sugar/caffeine across drinks).

docs.title: Gaps
docs.text:
• No dedicated "Topics Excluded" section (partial credit given based on related context elsewhere in the document).

  • Apply and Analyze outcomes are present but modest in count, reflecting the developmental level of the band (early elementary, identify/describe plus emerging comparison and simple demonstration) rather than a document defect.

  • Create-level outcomes remain explicitly deferred to Grade 4, which is appropriate for this band but caps rubric points under a generic scoring template designed for adult/higher-ed courses.

docs.title: Course Description — Grade 3
docs.text: This is the Grade 3 section of the Health Education intelligent textbook. It is one of 8 parallel grade-band sections (see the site-wide Course Description); each band has its own concept list, learning graph, chapters, quizzes, MicroSims, and infographics at a matching reading level. Source: 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards, Commissioner Approved (see references.md). Benchmark codes below (e.g. 3.1.1.1) are <grade>.<strand>.<anchor>.<seq>.

docs.title: Reading Level & Cognitive Demand
docs.text: Elementary, independent readers. This band introduces the first evaluative benchmarks (e.g., "evaluate personal behaviors to prevent injuries") and the first explicit mention of puberty as a body-change topic, alongside continued describe/explain work.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Grade 3 students (age ~8-9) and their teachers.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Grade 2 benchmarks across all 5 content strands, plus the Grade 2 skill benchmarks (explaining influences, using communication skills, describing decision options, goal-setting with reflection).

docs.title: Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band
docs.text:
A student arriving directly at Grade 3 without the K-2 sections should be briefly introduced to these ideas first:

  • Food groups and drink choices affect energy and growth; food safety practices exist for a reason.
  • Peer and family relationships can be healthy or unhealthy, and personal space/boundaries matter.
  • Emotions can be named, they influence behavior, and trusted adults or peers can help when someone is struggling.
  • Hygiene and environmental awareness (sun, noise, chemicals, water) protect the body; regular physical activity supports health.
  • Technology and touch both have safety rules, including saying no and knowing safe places/routines during emergencies.
  • A personal health goal can be set, acted on, and reflected on.

docs.title: Food and Nutrition
docs.text:
• Body signals for hunger and fullness (3.1.1.1)
  • Carbohydrates, protein, and fats on nutrition labels and how they help the body grow (3.1.1.2)
  • Why limiting caffeinated/sugary drinks matters; beverages that support energy, strength, and recovery for physical activity (3.1.1.3)
  • Food safety practices and preparation methods that promote healthy eating (3.1.1.4)

docs.title: Human Growth and Development
docs.text:
• Roles of family members and peers in healthy relationships (3.2.1.1)
  • Recognizing the stages of puberty and asking for help managing physical and emotional changes (3.2.1.2)

docs.title: Mental and Emotional Health
docs.text:
• Resilience and how personal choices affect mental/emotional wellbeing (3.3.1.1)
  • Coping with challenging situations and who to talk to (3.3.1.2)
  • Mental health challenges and their effects (3.3.1.3)
  • Empathy and how it supports friendships and care for others (3.3.1.4)
  • How emotions influence behavior, and how expressing emotions affects self and others (3.3.1.5)
  • How teasing, exclusion, or bullying affects individuals and community; treating all people of all abilities with kindness and respect (3.3.1.6)

docs.title: Personal Health and Wellness
docs.text:
• How different cultures/communities use traditional knowledge to protect the body from the environment (3.4.1.1)
  • Benefits of regular physical activity for health, mood, and learning; dressing appropriately for weather (3.4.1.2)
  • How cultural traditions and community practices prevent germ spread and why they work (3.4.1.3)

docs.title: Personal Safety and Violence Prevention
docs.text:
• How shared messages, images, or videos affect self/others; risks of sharing personal information (3.5.1.1)
  • Evaluating personal behaviors to prevent injuries across multiple environments (3.5.1.2)
  • How practicing safety procedures prepares students/staff for real emergencies; identifying trusted adults who can help (3.5.1.3)
  • The right to personal boundaries (3.5.1.4)

docs.title: Skill Standards
docs.text:
• Who can influence health practices and behaviors (3.7.2.1)
  • Determining the validity and reliability of health information, products, services, and other resources (3.7.3.1)
  • Verbal and nonverbal communication to express thoughts, feelings, wants, and needs, including in decision-making situations (3.7.4.1)
  • Expressing thoughts/feelings/wants/needs using I-statements, with support (3.7.4.2)
  • Identifying a personal health-related behavior to set a goal, and determining whether assistance/collaboration is needed (3.7.6.1)
  • Examining practices and behaviors that support health and wellbeing (3.7.7.1)
  • Identifying health topics relevant and meaningful to self/others (3.7.8.1)

docs.title: Key Vocabulary
docs.text: hunger/fullness signal, carbohydrate, protein, fat, nutrition label, puberty, resilience, empathy, mental health challenge, bullying, exclusion, personal boundary, validity/reliability of information, I-statement, injury prevention, safety procedure

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text: Outcomes below are grouped by Bloom's Taxonomy level and traced to their source benchmark codes. Grade 3 is the first band with genuine Evaluate-level benchmarks.

docs.title: 1. Remember
docs.text:
By the end of Grade 3, the student will be able to:

  1. Recall body signals for hunger and fullness (3.1.1.1).
  2. Recognize the stages of puberty (3.2.1.2).
  3. Recall ways to cope with challenging situations and who to talk to (3.3.1.2).
  4. Recall who can influence health practices and behaviors (3.7.2.1).
  5. Recall health topics relevant and meaningful to self and others (3.7.8.1).

docs.title: 2. Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain how carbohydrates, protein, and fats on nutrition labels help the body grow (3.1.1.2).
  2. Describe why it's important to limit caffeinated and sugary drinks (3.1.1.3).
  3. Describe food safety practices and preparation methods that promote healthy eating (3.1.1.4).
  4. Describe the roles of family members and peers in healthy relationships (3.2.1.1).
  5. Describe resilience and how personal choices impact mental/emotional wellbeing (3.3.1.1).
  6. Describe mental health challenges and their effects (3.3.1.3).
  7. Describe empathy and how it supports friendships and care for others (3.3.1.4).
  8. Explain how emotions influence behavior, and how expressing emotions affects oneself and others (3.3.1.5).
  9. Explain how teasing, exclusion, or bullying impacts wellbeing, and why treating all people with kindness and respect matters (3.3.1.6).
  10. Describe how different cultures and communities use traditional knowledge to protect the body from the environment (3.4.1.1).
  11. Explain the benefits of regular physical activity, including dressing appropriately for weather (3.4.1.2).
  12. Explain how cultural traditions and community practices prevent the spread of germs and why these practices work (3.4.1.3).
  13. Describe how shared messages, images, or videos affect self and others, and the risks of sharing personal information (3.5.1.1).
  14. Explain how practicing safety procedures prepares students and staff to respond in real emergencies (3.5.1.3).
  15. Describe the right to personal boundaries (3.5.1.4).

docs.title: 3. Apply
docs.text:
1. Demonstrate asking for help to manage physical and emotional changes during puberty (3.2.1.2).
  2. Demonstrate verbal and nonverbal communication skills to express thoughts, feelings, wants, and needs (3.7.4.1).
  3. Express thoughts, feelings, wants, and needs using I-statements, with support (3.7.4.2).

docs.title: 4. Analyze
docs.text:
1. Identify a personal health-related behavior to set a goal, and determine whether assistance or collaboration is needed (3.7.6.1).
  2. Examine practices and behaviors that support health and wellbeing (3.7.7.1).

docs.title: 5. Evaluate
docs.text:
1. Evaluate personal behaviors to prevent injuries across multiple environments (3.5.1.2).
  2. Determine the validity and reliability of health information, products, services, and other resources (3.7.3.1).

docs.title: 6. Create
docs.text: Grade 3 benchmarks do not yet include a design/construct task. Setting a goal and determining whether help is needed (3.7.6.1, listed under Analyze above) is the closest precursor — true goal-plan construction begins at Grade 4.

docs.title: Grade 3 Chapters
docs.text:
This section presents the Grade 3 Health Education material as eight chapters, arranged so that each chapter only relies on ideas introduced in earlier chapters. Read the chapters in order the first time through — later chapters (like Growth And Puberty and Communication And Goals) reuse ideas such as trusted adults and coping skills that are introduced earlier. Each chapter page lists its exact learning-graph concepts and links back to the chapter(s) it depends on, so you can jump back to review a prerequisite whenever something feels unfamiliar.

  1. Foundations Of Health — Introduces health as a foundation for the course and the skills for judging whether health information is trustworthy.
  2. Safety And Trusted Adults — Covers safe sharing of information, injury prevention, safety procedures, and the idea of a trusted adult.
  3. Wellness And Activity — Explores traditional health knowledge, physical activity, dressing for weather, and germ-prevention practices.
  4. Food And Nutrition — Covers hunger and fullness signals, nutrition labels, healthy beverage choices, and food safety.
  5. Relationships And Respect — Examines family and peer roles, personal boundaries, and the effects of bullying and exclusion.
  6. Growth And Puberty — Introduces puberty, its stages, and asking a trusted adult for help with body changes.
  7. Mental And Emotional Health — Builds resilience, coping skills, empathy, and understanding of mental health challenges.
  8. Communication And Goals — Practices verbal and nonverbal communication, I-statements, and setting a personal health goal.

docs.title: How To Use This Textbook
docs.text: Work through the chapters in numerical order the first time, since each one builds on concepts from the chapters before it. Every chapter page opens with a short summary and a numbered list of the exact concepts it covers, so you can preview what's ahead or search back for a specific term. The "Prerequisites" section at the bottom of each chapter links to the earlier chapter(s) it depends on — use those links to jump back and review before moving forward.

docs.text: This chapter introduces the overall idea of health as a foundation for everything else in the course. Students learn who and what can influence their health choices, and begin to ask whether health information, products, and services are trustworthy.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This is the first chapter in the Grade 3 course. It assumes only the bridging concepts described in the course description, including familiarity with food groups, relationships, emotions, hygiene, safety rules, and goal-setting from earlier grades.

Hi! I'm Scout.

Welcome to Grade 3 Health Education! I'm Scout, a friendly dog who loves helping kids make healthy choices. I'll be showing up all through this book, but I only ever do six jobs, and my pose tells you which one I'm doing:

  1. Welcome you at the start of every chapter — that's what I'm doing right now.
  2. Help you think about a big idea, using my thinking pose.
  3. Give you a tip — a small, handy trick to remember something.
  4. Warn you gently when something needs extra care or a grown-up's help.
  5. Encourage you when an idea feels new or a little tricky.
  6. Celebrate with you when you've learned something great.

That's it — six jobs, six poses. If I'm not doing one of those six things, I'm not in the chapter. Let's think it through together, friend. Healthy choices, happy you!

docs.title: What Is Health?
docs.text:
Health means how well a person's body and mind are working and feeling. It is bigger than just "not being sick." A healthy third grader eats food that helps them grow, moves their body every day, gets enough sleep, stays safe, and has ways to notice and share their feelings. Health also includes the people around a student — family, friends, and community — because no one builds healthy habits completely alone.

This year, students start asking a new kind of question: not just "What is healthy?" but "Is this actually true, and can I trust where it came from?" That second question is just as important as the first, and this chapter builds toward it step by step.

Think about a typical day. A student decides what to eat for breakfast, how to spend recess, whether to wear a jacket, and who to ask when they feel confused about something. Every one of those small decisions is a health behavior — an action that affects a person's physical, mental, or emotional well-being. This chapter looks closely at what shapes those everyday decisions.

Big Idea

Health is more than your body feeling fine. It's your body, your mind, your habits, and the people and messages around you — all working together.

Here are a few everyday examples that show how wide the idea of health really is:

  • Choosing water instead of a sugary drink before soccer practice.
  • Asking a trusted adult for help when a problem feels too big to solve alone.
  • Noticing that a friend copied their homework habits after watching an older sibling study.
  • Deciding whether a claim on a cereal box ("Gives you superpowers!") could possibly be true.

docs.title: Who and What Influences Health Behavior
docs.text:
No student makes health decisions in a bubble. Influences on health behavior are the people, places, and messages that shape the choices a person makes about their health — for better or for worse. Learning to notice these influences is the first step toward making thoughtful choices instead of automatic ones.

Common influences on a third grader's health behavior include:

  1. Family — the habits, rules, and traditions a student grows up with, like meal routines or bedtime.
  2. Friends and peers — what classmates eat, say, or do can make a habit feel normal or unusual.
  3. School — teachers, cafeteria menus, recess rules, and posters all send health messages.
  4. Community — coaches, neighbors, faith or cultural leaders, and local traditions.
  5. Media and advertising — commercials, packaging, apps, and shows that promote products or behaviors.
  6. Culture — a family or community's shared traditions around food, movement, and care.

Some influences push a student toward healthier choices, and some push away from them — and often the very same influence can do both at different times. A coach might encourage practice and rest equally; an advertisement might promote an exciting toy but also a sugary snack.

docs.title: Diagram: Who Shapes My Health Choices?
docs.text:
Who Shapes My Health Choices? Interactive Infographic

Type: infographic sim-id: health-influence-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: classify, exemplify, explain

Learning objective: Students classify everyday scenarios into the correct source of influence (family, friends, school, community, media, culture) and explain whether each example nudges a health behavior in a helpful or unhelpful direction.

Purpose: Help students see that health choices come from many outside sources, and that noticing the source is the first step toward evaluating whether to follow it.

Layout: A central child character surrounded by six labeled "influence bubbles" arranged in a ring: Family, Friends, School, Community, Media, Culture.

Interactive elements: - Click a bubble: an infobox opens with a short definition and two example scenario cards for that influence - Each scenario card has a thumbs-up or thumbs-down icon the student can pick, revealing a one-sentence explanation of why the example is helpful or unhelpful for health - "Show Another Example" button cycles a fresh scenario into the open bubble - A running tally at the bottom shows how many helpful vs. unhelpful examples the student has reviewed

Visual style: Flat, friendly illustration with the child character in the center and soft-colored bubbles radiating outward; diverse families and community settings represented.

Color scheme: Each influence bubble has its own soft color (family: warm yellow, friends: light green, school: blue, community: purple, media: orange, culture: teal) used consistently with later chapters.

Responsive behavior: Ring of bubbles collapses into a scrollable row on narrow screens; all bubbles remain tappable.

Implementation: p5.js with an object array of influence data (name, color, definition, scenario list) driving click-to-reveal infoboxes.

Helpful Tip

When something influences your health choice, ask yourself: "Is this helping my body and mind, or just grabbing my attention?" Naming the influence out loud makes it much easier to decide.

docs.title: Starting to Question What We Hear
docs.text:
Every day, students hear health claims from many sources: a doctor, a teacher, a commercial, a game app, a rumor from a friend, a label on a box. Not all of these claims deserve the same amount of trust. This year, students begin learning two related skills for judging health information: checking its validity and checking its reliability.

Validity of health information means whether a claim is actually true and based on real evidence — not made up, exaggerated, or misleading. A valid claim matches what real experts and real science have found. Reliability of health information means whether the source of the claim can be trusted consistently — because it comes from people with real training, honest intentions, and a track record of getting things right, not just one time, but again and again.

A simple way to picture the difference: validity asks "Is this particular fact true?" while reliability asks "Can I generally trust wherever this fact came from?" A source can even be reliable most of the time and still get one detail wrong — which is why good thinkers check both.

Third graders can start asking three simple questions about any health claim:

  • Who said it? A doctor, school nurse, or textbook is a very different source than an unfamiliar website, a stranger, or an advertisement.
  • Why did they say it? Is the goal to help people be healthy, or to sell something, get clicks, or just repeat a rumor?
  • Does it match what trusted adults and books say? If a claim sounds surprising, it is worth checking with a trusted adult, a doctor, or a reliable book before believing or repeating it.

Not Everything Is True

Some ads and rumors are designed to sound exciting, not to be true. If a health claim seems too good to be true — like a snack that gives "instant superpowers" — it probably is. Always check with a trusted adult, doctor, or book.

docs.title: Diagram: Trusted Source or Not?
docs.text:
Trusted Source or Not? MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: trusted-source-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Taxonomy: Evaluate (L5) Bloom Taxonomy Verb: judge, assess, validate

Learning objective: Students determine the validity and reliability of a simple health claim by evaluating its source and comparing it against what a trusted adult, doctor, or book would say.

Canvas layout: - Top area (150px): One health claim card shown at a time, with its source labeled (e.g., "School nurse says: wash your hands before eating," "Online ad says: this candy makes you run faster," "A book from the library says: sleep helps your brain grow") - Middle area (250px): Two labeled bins — "Trustworthy Source" and "Needs Checking" - Bottom strip (100px): Explanation caption and "Next Claim" button

Visual elements: - 8 claim cards cycling one at a time, mixing clearly trustworthy sources (doctor, school nurse, reliable book, parent) with clearly untrustworthy or unclear ones (online ad, unclear rumor, stranger's post, exaggerated commercial)

Interactive controls: - Click or drag the claim card into the matching bin - Button: "Next Claim" - Button: "Reset"

Default parameters: - First claim: "School nurse says: wash your hands before eating" (clear trustworthy example, to build confidence)

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the claim card with its stated source, no judgment yet Stage 2: After the student picks a bin, reveal whether the choice matches experts' view and a one-sentence reason ("A school nurse is trained to give health advice, so this is a trustworthy source.") Stage 3: Show a short reminder question: "Who said it, why did they say it, and does it match what trusted adults say?"

Behavior: - Correct placement: bin glows, gentle chime, reason caption appears - Incorrect placement: calm prompt, "Look again — who is giving this health claim, and why?" - After all claims, a summary caption reminds students that checking the source is the first step before believing or sharing a health claim

Instructional Rationale: Determining the validity and reliability of health information is Grade 3's first genuine Evaluate-level benchmark, so the pattern uses a judgment sorter with a revealed reason rather than passive viewing. Students must actively assess each source and compare it against a simple trusted standard, which matches the Evaluate-level demand of judging and validating.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Keep claim cards short and readable aloud. Avoid frightening or shaming language — the goal is confident, curious checking, not fear of every message.

docs.title: Comparing Validity and Reliability
docs.text:
It helps to see validity and reliability side by side, since third graders are just learning that these are two related but different checks.

Question What It Checks Example Is this specific fact true? Validity "Drinking water helps your body work well" matches what doctors and scientists know — it is valid. Can I trust this source in general? Reliability A school nurse or a well-known children's health book is a reliable source because they are trained and consistent. Who benefits if I believe this? Helps judge both An ad that benefits a company selling a product deserves extra checking before being trusted.

Notice that a single source, like a favorite book from the library, can be reliable overall while a single claim inside it should still be checked if it sounds surprising. Good health thinkers stay curious and check both the claim and the source — that habit protects them from being fooled by exciting-sounding but false information.

Asking Questions Is a Superpower

Learning to question a health claim is a brand-new skill this year, and it might feel a little strange to "doubt" something at first. That's completely normal — asking good questions is not being rude, it's being smart. You've got this!

docs.title: Bringing It All Together
docs.text:
Health is the big idea this whole book explores: how well a person's body and mind are working, growing, and feeling. This chapter showed that health behaviors don't happen in isolation — family, friends, school, community, media, and culture all shape the choices a student makes every day, sometimes helpfully and sometimes not. Because messages about health come from so many places, students are now ready to ask two connected questions about any health claim: is it valid (actually true), and does it come from a reliable source (one that can be trusted again and again)?

Every later Grade 3 chapter — food, growth and development, mental and emotional health, safety, and community practices — will return to these same ideas: what health means, who influences a health choice, and how to judge whether health information deserves to be trusted.

docs.title: Wrap-Up for Teachers
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter, most Grade 3 students should be able to describe health as covering body, mind, and relationships; name at least two influences on a health behavior and say whether each is generally helpful or unhelpful; and apply a simple three-question check (who said it, why, does it match trusted sources) to judge a health claim's validity and reliability. The MicroSims move from classification (influence explorer) to evaluation (trusted source sorter), matching the Grade 3 shift toward the band's first genuine Evaluate-level benchmark (3.7.3.1).

Chapter Complete!

You did it, friend! You now know what health really means, who influences your health choices, and how to check whether health information is valid and reliable. Keep asking good questions — we'll use these skills all through the book. Healthy choices, happy you!

Quick Check for Read-Aloud Time — Click to expand

Ask the class: "What two questions can we ask to check a health claim?" Then reveal: "Is it valid (actually true), and does it come from a reliable source (one we can trust again and again)?"

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Students explore how shared messages, images, and personal information can affect themselves and others, how to evaluate behaviors that prevent injuries, and how practicing safety procedures prepares everyone for real emergencies. The chapter also introduces the idea of a trusted adult who can help in difficult or unsafe situations.
