docs.title: Course Description — Grade 4
docs.text: This is the Grade 4 section of the Health Education intelligent textbook. It is one of 8 parallel grade-band sections (see the site-wide Course Description); each band has its own concept list, learning graph, chapters, quizzes, MicroSims, and infographics at a matching reading level. Source: 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards, Commissioner Approved (see references.md). Benchmark codes below (e.g. 4.1.1.1) are <grade>.<strand>.<anchor>.<seq>.

docs.title: Reading Level & Cognitive Demand
docs.text: Upper elementary. Benchmarks lean into plan, explain, analyze, and demonstrate refusal skills — the first appearance of refusal-skill language and of constructing a position from research. Per state requirements, mental health instruction becomes a required component starting at this band (2026-2027 school year, per references.md).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Grade 4 students (age ~9-10) and their teachers.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Grade 3 benchmarks across all 5 content strands, plus the Grade 3 skill benchmarks (identifying influences, judging information validity, using I-statements, setting a goal with a help/no-help decision).

docs.title: Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band
docs.text:
A student arriving directly at Grade 4 without the K-3 sections should be briefly introduced to these ideas first:

  • Nutrition labels list carbohydrates, protein, fat, and other nutrients; hydration and limiting sugary/caffeinated drinks matter.
  • Puberty is a stage of physical/emotional change that different people experience at different times, and it's normal to ask for help with it.
  • Emotions can be identified, they influence behavior, and mental health can be discussed openly with trusted adults.
  • Regular physical activity and basic hygiene/illness-prevention practices support long-term health.
  • Personal boundaries exist, sharing personal information online carries risk, and safety procedures/drills exist for real emergencies.
  • Health information should be checked for validity/reliability before it's trusted, and personal health goals can be set and pursued with or without help.

docs.title: Food and Nutrition
docs.text:
• Planning a balanced meal; how carbohydrates, protein, fats, vitamins, minerals, and water support the body; locating them on food labels (4.1.1.1)
  • Benefits of drinking enough water and limiting caffeinated/sugary drinks (4.1.1.2)
  • Effects of sugary and salty foods on health (4.1.1.3)
  • Safety practices for keeping food at safe temperatures (4.1.1.4)

docs.title: Human Growth and Development
docs.text:
• Managing conflicts respectfully across individuals and cultures (4.2.1.1)
  • Changes during puberty as a life stage observed across cultures, including Indigenous communities (4.2.1.2)

docs.title: Mental and Emotional Health (required instruction begins this band)
docs.text:
• How cultural practices and self-regulation benefit mental health (4.3.1.1)
  • Cultural practices and various methods for self-regulation (4.3.1.2)
  • How emotions affect behavior and strategies to manage them in healthy ways (4.3.1.3)
  • Healthy/safe ways to respond to teasing, exclusion, disagreements, bullying, unfair treatment, bias, and prejudice — witnessed or experienced (4.3.1.4)
  • Mental health can change over time like physical health; culturally appropriate and professional help is available (4.3.1.5)

docs.title: Personal Health and Wellness
docs.text:
• Common causes of allergic reactions and prevention/management strategies (4.4.1.1)
  • Cultural traditions (dance, community sports) as physical activity and their benefits to health, mood, and learning (4.4.1.2)
  • Infectious vs. non-infectious disease; how germs spread; prevention strategies, including cultural perspectives on wellness/caregiving (4.4.1.3)

docs.title: Personal Safety and Violence Prevention
docs.text:
• Harmful technology behavior and its impact on safety and mental health (4.5.1.1)
  • Situational awareness, recognizing harmful situations and exiting safely, and setting boundaries, including cultural/community perspectives (4.5.1.2)
  • Behaviors and warning signs that indicate someone/something is unsafe or dangerous (4.5.1.3)
  • Recognizing pressure from others and practicing strategies to assert choices safely (4.5.1.4)

docs.title: Skill Standards
docs.text:
• How family, peers, groups, culture, and media/technology influence practices and behaviors (4.7.2.1)
  • Characteristics of valid and reliable health information, products, and services (4.7.3.1)
  • Demonstrating refusal skills for a variety of situations and knowing when help is needed (4.7.4.1)
  • Developing a plan (actions, resources, progress tracking) toward a health-related goal, identifying supports and barriers (4.7.6.1)
  • Demonstrating and tracking practices/behaviors that support health and wellbeing (4.7.7.1)
  • Using research to construct a position on a relevant/meaningful health topic (4.7.8.1)

docs.title: Key Vocabulary
docs.text: macronutrient, vitamin, mineral, food temperature safety, puberty, conflict management, self-regulation, mental health, bias, prejudice, allergy, infectious disease, non-infectious disease, situational awareness, warning sign, peer pressure, refusal skill, valid/reliable information, goal plan

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text: Outcomes below are grouped by Bloom's Taxonomy level and traced to their source benchmark codes. Grade 4 is the first band with genuine Create-level benchmarks (planning, developing, constructing).

docs.title: 1. Remember
docs.text:
By the end of Grade 4, the student will be able to:

  1. Recall cultural practices and methods for self-regulation (4.3.1.2).
  2. Recall common causes of allergic reactions (4.4.1.1).
  3. Recall behaviors and warning signs that could indicate someone is unsafe or that a situation could become dangerous (4.5.1.3).

docs.title: 2. Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain how carbohydrates, protein, fats, vitamins, minerals, and water support the body (4.1.1.1).
  2. Summarize the benefits of drinking enough water and limiting caffeinated/sugary drinks (4.1.1.2).
  3. Describe the effects of sugary and salty foods on health (4.1.1.3).
  4. Explain safety practices for keeping food at safe temperatures (4.1.1.4).
  5. Explain how to manage conflicts respectfully across individuals and cultures (4.2.1.1).
  6. Describe the changes that occur during puberty as a life stage observed across cultures, including Indigenous communities (4.2.1.2).
  7. Explain how emotions affect behavior and identify strategies to manage them in healthy ways (4.3.1.3).
  8. Describe that mental health, like physical health, can change over time, and that culturally appropriate and professional help is available (4.3.1.5).
  9. Describe strategies to prevent or manage allergic reactions (4.4.1.1).
  10. Explain how engaging in cultural traditions such as dance and community sports provides physical-activity benefits (4.4.1.2).
  11. Explain the difference between infectious and non-infectious diseases and how prevention strategies reduce illness (4.4.1.3).
  12. Explain how family, peers, groups, culture, and media/technology influence practices and behaviors (4.7.2.1).
  13. Describe characteristics of valid and reliable health information, products, and services (4.7.3.1).

docs.title: 3. Apply
docs.text:
1. Demonstrate healthy and safe ways to respond when experiencing or witnessing teasing, exclusion, bullying, unfair treatment, bias, or prejudice (4.3.1.4).
  2. Practice strategies to assert personal choices safely when pressured by others (4.5.1.4).
  3. Demonstrate refusal skills in a variety of situations (4.7.4.1).
  4. Demonstrate and track practices and behaviors that support health and wellbeing (4.7.7.1).

docs.title: 4. Analyze
docs.text:
1. Analyze examples of harmful behavior when using technology and explain the impact on safety and mental health (4.5.1.1).
  2. Analyze strategies for developing situational awareness, recognizing harmful situations, safely exiting them, and setting boundaries (4.5.1.2).

docs.title: 5. Evaluate
docs.text: 1. Describe and evaluate how cultural practices and self-regulation benefit mental health (4.3.1.1).

docs.title: 6. Create
docs.text:
1. Plan a balanced meal using foods from different food groups and locate nutrients on food labels (4.1.1.1).
  2. Develop a goal plan that includes actions, resources, and progress-tracking, and identify supports and barriers (4.7.6.1).
  3. Use research to construct a position on a relevant, meaningful health topic (4.7.8.1).

docs.title: Grade 4 Chapters
docs.text:
This section presents the Grade 4 health education content as six chapters, sequenced so that each chapter builds only on concepts introduced earlier. Read them in order the first time through — later chapters (especially Health Literacy and Goal Setting) assume ideas from Food and Nutrition, Growth and Development, and Wellness and Disease Prevention. Each chapter lists the concepts it covers and links to the earlier chapter(s) it depends on, so you can jump back to review a prerequisite if a topic feels unfamiliar.

  1. Food and Nutrition — Introduces health itself, then the nutrients that fuel the body, nutrition labels, balanced meal planning, hydration, and food safety.
  2. Growth and Development Across Cultures — Respectful conflict management and puberty as a life stage observed across cultures, including Indigenous communities.
  3. Mental and Emotional Health — Self-regulation, managing emotions, recognizing bias and prejudice, and responding safely to teasing and bullying.
  4. Personal Safety and Refusal Skills — Influences on behavior, situational awareness, boundaries, warning signs, peer pressure, and refusal skills.
  5. Wellness and Disease Prevention — Allergies, cultural physical-activity traditions, and infectious versus non-infectious disease prevention.
  6. Health Literacy and Goal Setting — Evaluating health information and products, constructing a research-based position, and building a personal health goal plan.

docs.title: How to Use This Textbook
docs.text: Each chapter page opens with a short summary and a numbered list of the concepts it covers, so you can preview what you'll learn before reading. Work through the chapters in order, since each one lists the earlier chapter(s) its ideas depend on. Diagrams, MicroSims, and practice questions inside each chapter are there to help you actively use the ideas, not just read about them — pause and try them before moving on.

docs.title: Learning Graph — Grade 4
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for the Grade 4 band of the Health Education intelligent textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this band. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the band. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

This band's graph is intentionally smaller than a general-purpose graph — 58 concepts rather than 200 — because Grade 4 health benchmarks are plan/explain/analyze-level content, with the first genuine create-level reasoning (meal planning, goal-plan development, research-based positions) and the start of required mental-health instruction, for 9-10 year olds (see the Course Description Assessment for the rationale). It builds directly on the Kindergarten (45-concept), Grade 1 (55-concept), Grade 2 (55-concept), and Grade 3 (57-concept) bands' graphs and uses the same 7-category taxonomy for cross-band comparability.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this band. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Grade 4 course description is a well-structured, standards-traceable document derived from the 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards. It enumerates 25 benchmark-coded topics across five content strands (Food and Nutrition, Human Growth and Development, Mental and Emotional Health, Personal Health and Wellness, Personal Safety and Violence Prevention) plus a cross-cutting Skill Standards group, and organizes learning outcomes using the full 2001 Bloom's Taxonomy (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create). This assessment evaluates the description against a right-sized concept target of approximately 55-60 concepts, not the skill's generic 200-concept default, which would force invented content not grounded in the standards.

Grade 4 is a meaningful developmental step up from Grade 3: it marks the start of required mental-health instruction (per state requirements effective 2026-2027), introduces the first genuine refusal-skill language, the first explicit peer-pressure vocabulary, and — notably — the first genuine Create-level benchmarks (planning a balanced meal, developing a goal plan, constructing a research-based position), which Grade 3 explicitly deferred.

docs.title: Strengths
docs.text:
• Every topic traces to a specific MDE benchmark code, giving the learning graph strong provenance.

  • First band with genuine, well-formed Create-level outcomes (meal planning, goal-plan development, research-based position construction), closing the gap Grade 3 explicitly left open.

  • Clear five-strand + Skill Standards structure maps cleanly onto the same taxonomy scheme used for Kindergarten through Grade 3, supporting cross-band comparability.

  • Key Vocabulary section (19 terms) gives ready-made concept candidates, including new terms (peer pressure, refusal skill, bias, prejudice) not seen in earlier bands.

  • Explicit "Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band" section clarifies which K-3 ideas are assumed but not re-taught.

  • Documents the transition to required mental-health instruction beginning this band, an important structural marker for the Mental and Emotional Health category.

docs.title: Gaps
docs.text:
• No dedicated "Topics Excluded" section (partial credit given based on related context elsewhere in the document).

  • Evaluate-level outcomes are present but limited to a single outcome, reflecting the developmental level of the band rather than a document defect — Grade 4 is still building toward the fuller evaluate/synthesize work of later grades.

  • Remember-level outcomes, while sufficient, are the thinnest of the six Bloom tiers (3 outcomes, at the minimum threshold).

docs.title: Course Description — Grade 5
docs.text: This is the Grade 5 section of the Health Education intelligent textbook. It is one of 8 parallel grade-band sections (see the site-wide Course Description); each band has its own concept list, learning graph, chapters, quizzes, MicroSims, and infographics at a matching reading level. Source: 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards, Commissioner Approved (see references.md). Benchmark codes below (e.g. 5.1.1.1) are <grade>.<strand>.<anchor>.<seq>. This is the last individually-graded band before the standards shift to grade bands (6-8, 9-12).

docs.title: Reading Level & Cognitive Demand
docs.text: Upper elementary, transitioning toward middle-school-style comparison and application. Benchmarks emphasize compare, use, apply, evaluate, and demonstrate — e.g., comparing nutrition labels between two foods, evaluating strategies for recognizing unhealthy relationships.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Grade 5 students (age ~10-11) and their teachers.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Grade 4 benchmarks across all 5 content strands, plus the Grade 4 skill benchmarks (explaining influences, describing information validity, demonstrating refusal skills, goal planning with barriers/supports).

docs.title: Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band
docs.text:
A student arriving directly at Grade 5 without the K-4 sections should be briefly introduced to these ideas first:

  • Nutrition labels and food groups guide meal choices; caffeinated/sugary drinks and unsafe food handling carry health risks.
  • Puberty involves physical/emotional change, and family/peer relationships influence feelings, behavior, and decisions.
  • Mental health can be supported through self-regulation and cultural practices, and it's normal and healthy to ask a trusted adult for help.
  • Bullying, exclusion, and unfair treatment harm mental health and belonging regardless of ability.
  • Regular physical activity, allergy awareness, and disease-prevention habits (hygiene, safe food/water) support long-term health.
  • Refusal skills, setting/respecting boundaries, and recognizing warning signs of unsafe situations are learnable skills, not just instincts.
  • A health-related goal can be planned with actions, resources, and known barriers, then tracked over time.

docs.title: Food and Nutrition
docs.text:
• Comparing cultural approaches to meeting daily nutrient/energy needs (5.1.1.1)
  • Using nutrition labels to compare two similar foods and choose the healthier one (5.1.1.2)
  • Comparing water to other drinks and how choosing water supports health (5.1.1.3)
  • Applying nutritious eating strategies to plan and choose meals/snacks (5.1.1.4)
  • How unsafe food practices cause foodborne illness (5.1.1.5)

docs.title: Human Growth and Development
docs.text:
• How family and peer relationships influence feelings, behavior, and decision-making (5.2.1.1)
  • Effectively telling a trusted adult about a health concern or question, for yourself or someone else (5.2.1.2)

docs.title: Mental and Emotional Health
docs.text:
• Healthy/restorative strategies for managing personal growth and relationships (5.3.1.1)
  • Supporting a peer in a difficult situation while respecting boundaries and guiding them to seek help (5.3.1.2)
  • Including and supporting others to promote equity and belonging (5.3.1.3)
  • Situations, people, and experiences that influence emotions, and how emotions influence behavior (5.3.1.4)
  • How individual actions and bystander behaviors can prevent or reduce bullying, fighting, and violence (5.3.1.5)
  • How treating people of all abilities with kindness supports an inclusive, welcoming environment (5.3.1.6)

docs.title: Personal Health and Wellness
docs.text:
• Why adequate sleep and rest matter for growth, learning, and wellbeing (5.4.1.1)
  • How different physical activities support different fitness components; identifying one activity per component (5.4.1.2)
  • Signs of allergic reactions and how to respond (5.4.1.3)
  • Symptoms of common illnesses/chronic conditions, when to seek help, and how personal behaviors affect long-term health (5.4.1.4)

docs.title: Personal Safety and Violence Prevention
docs.text:
• How technology and social media can cause harm; prevention/reporting strategies (5.5.1.1)
  • Recognizing unhealthy/harmful relationships, setting boundaries, seeking support, and safely exiting when needed (5.5.1.2)
  • Individual, peer, and school-staff actions that reduce risk during an emergency (5.5.1.3)
  • The difference between consent and coercion; situations that feel unsafe and how to report to a trusted adult (5.5.1.4)

docs.title: Skill Standards
docs.text:
• Strategies and resources to manage influences that impact health practices/behaviors (5.7.2.1)
  • Determining which trusted adults/individuals/resources are needed for various situations (5.7.3.1)
  • Demonstrating conflict-resolution skills to prevent/manage/resolve conflict (5.7.4.1)
  • Demonstrating boundary-setting skills for self and others (5.7.4.2)
  • Examining options and consequences affecting health-related outcomes (5.7.5.1)

  • Delivering messages to various audiences and examining outcomes (5.7.8.1)

docs.text: Outcomes below are grouped by Bloom's Taxonomy level and traced to their source benchmark codes.

  2. Explain how family and peer relationships influence feelings, behavior, and decision-making (5.2.1.1).

  5. Explain how treating people of all abilities with kindness supports an inclusive, welcoming environment (5.3.1.6).
  6. Explain why adequate sleep and rest are important for healthy growth and learning (5.4.1.1).

  2. Demonstrate supporting a peer in a difficult situation while respecting boundaries and guiding them to seek help (5.3.1.2).

1. Compare cultural approaches to meeting daily nutrient and energy needs (5.1.1.1).
  2. Use nutrition labels to compare two similar foods and determine which is healthier (5.1.1.2).
  3. Compare water to other drinks and explain how choosing water supports health (5.1.1.3).
  4. Analyze how individual actions and bystander behaviors can prevent or reduce bullying, fighting, and violence (5.3.1.5).
  5. Identify strategies and resources to manage influences that impact health practices and behaviors (5.7.2.1).
  6. Examine options and consider consequences that may affect health-related outcomes (5.7.5.1).
  7. Analyze the impact of health practices and behaviors and explain the importance of taking ownership of personal health (5.7.7.1).

docs.title: 5. Evaluate
docs.text:
1. Evaluate ways technology and social media can cause harm and identify strategies for prevention and reporting (5.5.1.1).
  2. Evaluate strategies for recognizing unhealthy or harmful relationships, setting boundaries, seeking support, and safely exiting when needed (5.5.1.2).
  3. Determine which trusted adults, other individuals, and health resources are needed for various situations (5.7.3.1).
  4. Reflect on the results of a health-related decision and its impact (5.7.5.2).
  5. Track progress and reflect on achieving a personal health goal (5.7.6.1).

docs.text: 1. Apply nutritious eating strategies to plan and choose meals and snacks (5.1.1.4).

docs.title: Grade 5 Chapters
docs.text:
This section contains the 7 chapters of the Grade 5 Health Education band. Each chapter builds on concepts introduced in earlier chapters, so the chapters are best read in order the first time through — but once you've completed the band, feel free to jump directly to whichever chapter you need to review. Every chapter opens with a short summary and a list of the concepts it covers, and closes with a link back to the earlier chapters it depends on, so you can always trace an idea back to where it was first introduced.

  1. Foundations And Trusted Adults — Introduces health itself, how family and peers shape decisions and emotions, and how to identify and tell a trusted adult about a health concern.
  2. Food And Nutrition — Compares cultural approaches to nutrition, teaches label reading and water choice, and covers meal planning and foodborne illness prevention.
  3. Managing Emotions And Relationships — Builds restorative self-management strategies and skills for supporting peers while respecting boundaries and recognizing emotional triggers.
  4. Equity, Belonging, And Bystander Action — Explores equity, belonging, and ability-inclusive kindness alongside bystander strategies for preventing bullying and violence.
  5. Personal Health And Wellness — Covers sleep, fitness components, allergic reactions, chronic conditions, and how personal behaviors shape long-term health.
  6. Personal Safety And Violence Prevention — Addresses technology and social media harm, unhealthy relationships, consent versus coercion, and emergency risk reduction.
  7. Health Skills And Goal Setting — Ties together conflict resolution, boundary-setting, decision reflection, goal tracking, and delivering a health message.

docs.title: How To Use This Textbook
docs.text: Read each chapter's Summary and Concepts Covered list before diving into the content so you know what to expect. If a term or idea feels unfamiliar, check the Prerequisites section at the bottom of the chapter — it links directly to the earlier chapter where that concept was first taught. Diagrams, MicroSims, and practice questions throughout each chapter are meant to be explored interactively, not just read, so take the time to click, test, and experiment as you go.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This opening chapter grounds the Grade 5 band in the idea of health itself and in the people and relationships that shape a student's choices. Students examine how family and peer relationships influence feelings, behavior, and decisions, and how emotions in turn shape behavior. The chapter closes by building the skill of identifying a trusted adult and telling that adult about a health concern, a skill referenced throughout every later chapter.

docs.title: Learning Graph — Grade 5
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for the Grade 5 band of the Health Education intelligent textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this band. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the band. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

This band's graph is intentionally smaller than a general-purpose graph — 70 concepts rather than 200 — because Grade 5 health benchmarks, while the richest and most granular of the K-5 bands (31 benchmark-coded topics), are still scoped to upper-elementary compare/apply/evaluate-level content for 10-11 year olds (see the Course Description Assessment for the rationale). Grade 5 is the last individually-graded band before the 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards shift to grade spans (6-8, 9-12). It builds directly on the Kindergarten (45-concept), Grade 1 (55-concept), Grade 2 (55-concept), Grade 3 (57-concept), and Grade 4 (58-concept) bands' graphs and uses the same 7-category taxonomy for cross-band comparability.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this band. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Grade 5 course description is a well-structured, standards-traceable document derived from the 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards. It enumerates 31 benchmark-coded topics across five content strands (Food and Nutrition, Human Growth and Development, Mental and Emotional Health, Personal Health and Wellness, Personal Safety and Violence Prevention) plus a cross-cutting Skill Standards group — the richest topic set of the K-5 bands — and organizes learning outcomes using the full 2001 Bloom's Taxonomy (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create). This assessment evaluates the description against a right-sized concept target of approximately 65-70 concepts, not the skill's generic 200-concept default, which would force invented content not grounded in the standards.

Grade 5 is the last individually-graded band before the 2025 Minnesota standards shift to multi-grade spans (6-8, 9-12), and the document notes this explicitly. It also introduces the first genuine consent and coercion language, the first explicit equity and belonging vocabulary tied to ability-inclusive treatment, and continues the comparison/analysis emphasis (comparing nutrition labels, comparing cultural approaches to nutrient needs) that began developing in Grade 4.

docs.title: Strengths
docs.text:
• Every topic traces to a specific MDE benchmark code, giving the learning graph strong provenance.

  • Largest and most granular topic set of any K-5 band (31 benchmark-coded topics), reflecting Grade 5's role as the capstone of individually-graded elementary standards.

  • Strongest Evaluate-level tier of the K-5 bands (5 outcomes), reflecting the band's shift toward middle-school-style judgment and comparison (evaluating relationship safety, technology harm, resource selection).

  • Introduces new, more mature vocabulary not seen in earlier bands: consent, coercion, equity, belonging, bystander, fitness component — each mapping to a specific benchmark.

  • Clear five-strand + Skill Standards structure maps cleanly onto the same taxonomy scheme used for Kindergarten through Grade 4, supporting cross-band comparability.

  • Explicit "Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band" section clarifies which K-4 ideas are assumed but not re-taught.

  • Explicitly documents its own status as the last individually-graded band before the standards shift to grade spans, an important structural marker for the whole K-5 sequence.

docs.title: Gaps
docs.text:
• No dedicated "Topics Excluded" section (partial credit given based on related context elsewhere in the document).

  • Remember-level outcomes are limited to a single outcome, the thinnest Remember tier of any band generated so far — though this reflects Grade 5's developmental shift toward comparison/application rather than rote recall, not a document defect.

  • Create-level outcomes are thinner than Grade 4's (1 vs. 3), reflecting that most of Grade 5's higher-order benchmarks land at Analyze/Evaluate (comparison, judgment) rather than Create (synthesis/production).

  • The course description contains an explicit inline note that its Personal Health/Wellness and Personal Safety strand benchmarks were sampled and should be double-checked against the primary source. Per this run's instructions, the content actually present in the file is treated as authoritative and complete for concept-graph generation; no additional benchmarks were invented to compensate.

docs.title: Concept Count Guidance
docs.text: Per explicit run-level override, this band targets approximately 65-70 concepts (not 200), built only from the 31 enumerated benchmarks, the 13 key vocabulary terms, and a small number of clearly-implied bridging/connective concepts. This is appropriate given Grade 5's richer benchmark set (the largest of the K-5 bands) and keeps the graph comparable in density and structure to the Kindergarten (45-concept), Grade 1 (55-concept), Grade 2 (55-concept), Grade 3 (57-concept), and Grade 4 (58-concept) bands already generated, while reflecting the larger source material with a proportionally larger graph.

docs.title: Course Description — Grades 6-8
docs.text: This is the Grades 6-8 section of the Health Education intelligent textbook. It is one of 8 parallel grade-band sections (see the site-wide Course Description); each band has its own concept list, learning graph, chapters, quizzes, MicroSims, and infographics at a matching reading level. Source: 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards, Commissioner Approved (see references.md). Benchmark codes below (e.g. 6.1.1.1) are <grade band>.<strand>.<anchor>.<seq>. This is the first band graded as a span rather than a single grade — benchmarks apply across all three grades (6, 7, 8) rather than being individually leveled.

docs.title: Reading Level & Cognitive Demand
docs.text:
Middle school. This band introduces two entirely new elements not present in K-5:

  • Sexual Health is added to the Human Growth and Development strand (now "Human Growth and Development and Sexual Health").
  • Substance Use Awareness and Prevention appears for the first time as its own strand (not taught below grade 6). Per state requirements, cannabis/substance-use prevention curriculum is required starting the 2026-2027 school year at this band.

Cognitive demand shifts to analyze, evaluate, and design — e.g., analyzing dietary guidelines across cultures, evaluating warning signs for suicide/self-harm risk and knowing when to seek help. Note also that Appendix A of the source standards lists statewide-mandated topics that land substantially in this band: vaping awareness/prevention, cannabis/fentanyl and other substance use, and STI/HIV/HPV prevention (see references.md).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Grade 6-8 students (age ~11-14) and their teachers.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Grade 5 benchmarks across Food and Nutrition, Human Growth and Development, Mental and Emotional Health, Personal Health and Wellness, and Personal Safety and Violence Prevention. Substance Use Awareness and Prevention has no K-5 prerequisite — it begins at this band.

docs.title: Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band
docs.text:
A student entering directly at Grade 6-8 without the K-5 sections should be briefly introduced to these ideas first, since this band assumes them without re-teaching:

  • Reading and comparing nutrition labels; the health effects of sugary, salty, and caffeinated foods/drinks.
  • Family and peer relationships can be healthy or unhealthy; consent and coercion are different things; personal boundaries can be set and communicated.
  • Emotions influence behavior, mental health can be discussed openly, and trusted adults or professionals can help with a mental or emotional health concern — including a concern about suicide or self-harm.
  • Bullying, exclusion, and bias harm mental health and belonging; bystander actions can prevent or reduce violence.
  • Basic disease prevention (hygiene, safe food/water) and the components of physical fitness.
  • Refusal skills, boundary-setting, and recognizing warning signs of unsafe situations, both in person and online/via technology.
  • Goal-setting with a plan, resources, and known barriers, tracked and reflected on over time.

Because this band introduces Sexual Health and Substance Use for the first time, no prior-band bridging is possible for those two areas — they should be treated as genuinely new content for every student regardless of prior band completion.

docs.text:
• Analyzing dietary guidelines that meet the needs of various cultures and communities (6.1.1.1)

docs.text:

docs.title: Grade 6-8 Health Education — Chapters
docs.text: This section contains the chapter-by-chapter content for the Grade 6-8 band of the Health Education intelligent textbook. Chapters are sequenced so that each one builds on the concepts introduced earlier — start at Chapter 1 and move forward in order, or use the learning graph to jump to a specific concept and trace its prerequisites. Each chapter lists the concepts it covers and the earlier chapters it depends on, so you can review a prerequisite chapter if a topic feels unfamiliar.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text:
1. Health Foundations And Nutrition — Establishes what health means and builds skills for reading food labels, comparing dietary guidelines across cultures, and understanding food sovereignty and community food access.
  2. Relationships, Boundaries, And Consent — Explores relationship structures, healthy versus unhealthy relationship dynamics, personal boundary-setting, and the critical distinction between consent and coercion.
  3. Healthcare Access And Sexual Health — Covers how adolescents access comprehensive health care and understand STIs, HIV, treatment options, and strategies for preventing infection and unintended pregnancy.
  4. Emotional Well-Being And Mental Health — Introduces warning signs for suicide, self-harm, and emotional distress alongside empathy, communication, and healthy strategies for managing stress and resolving conflict.
  5. Stigma, Bias, And Brain Health — Examines how bias, exclusion, and bullying affect mental health, how media representation reduces stigma, and what keeps the brain healthy, including Alzheimer's and dementia.
  6. Sleep, Fitness, And Emergency Response — Builds skills in sleep habits, workout planning, emergency medication use and the Heimlich maneuver, and recognizing and responding to emergencies.
  7. Digital Safety And School Safety — Addresses digital risks such as sharing explicit content, power dynamics, and peer pressure, plus the collective actions that keep schools safe.
  8. Substances And The Developing Brain — Details how alcohol, tobacco, nicotine, cannabis, and other drugs affect the developing brain and body, and the cultural teachings that protect youth.
  9. Substance Use Culture, Safety, And Risk — Covers commercial tobacco addiction, safe medication storage and disposal, and the elevated injury, violence, and health risks tied to substance use.
  10. Substance Use Disorder, Recovery, And Policy — Explains substance use disorder, relapse, treatment, community recovery supports, impaired driving risk, and the industry advertising that shapes health disparities.
  11. Health Influences And Information Literacy — Opens the cross-cutting Skill Standards strand: analyzing social, cultural, and media influences on health practices, and accessing and evaluating valid health information.
  12. Advocacy, Goal Setting, And Health Messaging — Develops communication, conflict-resolution, self-advocacy, and refusal skills, then applies them to goal-setting, decision-making, and designing health messages for real audiences.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter introduces the concept of health as a foundation for the entire course and turns to the Food and Nutrition strand. Students learn to analyze dietary guidelines across cultures, read and evaluate food labels and marketing claims, and compare the effects of water, sugary drinks, and caffeinated beverages on the body. The chapter closes by connecting meal and snack planning to food sovereignty and community efforts that increase access to healthy food.

docs.title: Learning Graph — Grade 6-8
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for the Grade 6-8 band of the Health Education intelligent textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this band. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the band. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

This band's graph is substantially larger than the K-5 bands' graphs — 133 concepts, roughly double Grade 5's 70 — because Grade 6-8 is the first band graded as a 3-grade span rather than a single grade, and the first band where Sexual Health (added to Human Growth and Development) and Substance Use Awareness and Prevention (an entirely new strand) appear (see the Course Description Assessment for the rationale). It builds directly on the Kindergarten through Grade 5 bands' graphs for the five strands they share, and introduces genuinely new content for Sexual Health and Substance Use Awareness, which have no true prior-band bridge.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this band. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy — Grade 6-8
docs.text:
This band introduces an eighth category not present in the K-5 bands: Substance Use Awareness and Prevention (SUB), a wholly new strand at Grade 6-8. The Human Growth and Development category is renamed GROW (Human Growth, Development, and Sexual Health) to reflect the addition of Sexual Health content at this band. Skill Standards (SKIL) remains a single category because, at 25 of 133 concepts (18.8%), it stays comfortably under the 30% balance ceiling even though its raw benchmark count (19) is the largest Skill Standards set in the series so far.

Category TaxonomyID Description Foundations FOUND Bridging/anchor concepts carried forward from earlier bands that connect concepts across strands (e.g., "Health"). Food and Nutrition FOOD Dietary guidelines, food labels and marketing claims, drink choices, meal/snack planning, and food sovereignty/community food access. Human Growth, Development, and Sexual Health GROW Relationship structures and characteristics, seeking help about development/relationships, comprehensive health care access, STIs/HIV, pregnancy prevention, healthcare barriers, boundaries, consent, and coercion. Mental and Emotional Health EMOT Suicide/self-harm warning signs, stress, emotional distress, empathy and conflict resolution, emotion management, exclusion/bullying/bias effects, media representation, brain health, and dementia. Personal Health and Wellness WELL Sleep, fitness/workout planning, emergency medication use and the Heimlich maneuver, emergency recognition and scene safety, and infectious disease prevention. Personal Safety and Violence Prevention SAFE Harmful/explicit content sharing, power dynamics and peer pressure, digital communication risk, school safety actions, and consent/coercion in the safety context. Substance Use Awareness and Prevention SUB Alcohol, tobacco, nicotine, cannabis, and other drug effects; medication safety; substance use disorder and relapse; impaired driving; industry advertising influence; and cultural/traditional context for substance use. Skill Standards SKIL Cross-cutting skills: identifying influences, accessing/evaluating health information, communication, conflict resolution, self-advocacy, refusal skills, decision-making, goal-setting, ownership of health behaviors, and health message design.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Grade 6-8 course description is the most extensive and structurally mature document produced so far in this series. It is derived from the 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards and enumerates 59 benchmark-coded topics across six content strands (Food and Nutrition; Human Growth, Development, and Sexual Health; Mental and Emotional Health; Personal Health and Wellness; Personal Safety and Violence Prevention; and the entirely new Substance Use Awareness and Prevention strand) plus a large cross-cutting Skill Standards group (19 benchmarks). This is nearly double the topic count of Grade 5 (31 benchmarks), consistent with Grade 6-8 being graded as a three-grade span rather than a single grade.

This assessment evaluates the description against a right-sized concept target of approximately 120-135 concepts (not the skill's generic 200-concept default), reflecting a proportional scale-up from the K-5 bands while avoiding invented content not grounded in the standards.

docs.title: Strengths
docs.text:
• Every topic traces to a specific MDE benchmark code, giving the learning graph strong provenance — 59 topic benchmarks plus 19 Skill Standards benchmarks (78 total), roughly double Grade 5's 31.

  • Largest and most granular topic set of the series, reflecting the shift to a 3-grade span (6, 7, 8) rather than a single grade.

  • Explicitly documents the two structurally new elements at this band — Sexual Health folded into Human Growth and Development, and Substance Use Awareness and Prevention as a brand-new strand — with clear rationale (state mandate effective 2026-2027) and clear signaling that no K-5 bridging exists for these two areas.

  • Strongest combined Analyze/Understand tiers in the series (21 outcomes each), matching the standards' own repeated "apply skill cues to analyze" phrasing.

  • Strongest Create tier of the series (5 outcomes vs. Grade 5's 1), reflecting the band's shift toward designing workout plans, meal plans, goal plans, and health messages.

  • Detailed "Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band" section explicitly separates content that carries forward from K-5 (nutrition labels, consent/boundaries, emotions/mental health, bullying/bystander action, fitness, refusal skills, goal-setting) from content that is genuinely new at this band (Sexual Health, Substance Use).

  • Cross-references Appendix A (statewide-mandated topics: vaping, cannabis/ fentanyl, STI/HIV/HPV prevention) which land substantially in this band, strengthening traceability to the primary standards document.

docs.title: Gaps
docs.text:
• No dedicated "Topics Excluded" section (partial credit given based on related context in the Reading Level & Cognitive Demand section).

  • Remember-level outcomes are limited to 3, thinner than Understand/Analyze — but this is an accurate reflection of the standards' own emphasis on higher-order cognitive demand at this band, not a document defect.

  • Evaluate-level outcomes (2) are the thinnest Bloom's tier in this document, though Analyze-level outcomes at this band frequently blend in evaluative language ("analyze and evaluate a thoughtful decision-making process") which somewhat compensates.

docs.title: Concept Count Guidance
docs.text: Per explicit run-level override, this band targets approximately 120-135 concepts (not 200), built from the 59 enumerated topic benchmarks, the 19 Skill Standards benchmarks, the 26 Key Vocabulary terms, and a small number of clearly-implied bridging/connective concepts carried forward from Grade 5. This roughly doubles Grade 5's 70-concept graph, proportional to the near-doubling of benchmark count (31 to 59 topic benchmarks) and the addition of a wholly new strand (Substance Use Awareness and Prevention).

docs.title: Overall Quality Score: 92 / 100
docs.text: This score is above both the skill's general 70-point proceed threshold and its 80-point "good quality" guidance, and is the highest score in this series to date. Proceeding automatically with learning graph generation per run authorization (unattended run — no user pause required).

docs.title: Course Description — Grades 9-12
docs.text: This is the Grades 9-12 section of the Health Education intelligent textbook. It is one of 8 parallel grade-band sections (see the site-wide Course Description); each band has its own concept list, learning graph, chapters, quizzes, MicroSims, and infographics at a matching reading level. Source: 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards, Commissioner Approved (see references.md). Benchmark codes below (e.g. 9.1.1.1) are <grade band>.<strand>.<anchor>.<seq>. This is the terminal band and a grade span (9-12), matching the highest cognitive demand in the standards.

docs.title: Reading Level & Cognitive Demand
docs.text: High school. Cognitive demand peaks here: design, evaluate, synthesize, apply across contexts. Benchmarks require students to construct plans (e.g., a personal nutrition plan), evaluate evidence (e.g., beverage choices using hydration/sugar/caffeine data), and reason about systemic and cultural factors (e.g., how income and food systems affect chronic-disease risk). Appendix A of the source standards lists statewide-mandated topics that culminate in this band: CPR/AED, vaping awareness/prevention, cannabis and other substance use (including fentanyl), STI/HIV/HPV prevention, and mental health education including suicide/self-harm prevention (see references.md).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Grade 9-12 students (age ~14-18) and their teachers. This is also the band most directly relevant to career/college/community readiness framing per the standards' introduction.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Grade 6-8 benchmarks across all 6 strands, including the 6-8 introduction of Sexual Health and Substance Use Awareness and Prevention.

docs.title: Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band
docs.text:
A student entering directly at Grade 9-12 without any earlier band should be briefly introduced to these ideas first, since this band assumes them without re-teaching:

  • Reading nutrition labels and evaluating dietary guidelines across cultures; how food systems and income relate to health.
  • Relationship structures vary across individuals and cultures; consent is central to healthy relationships; STIs/HIV exist, are transmitted in known ways, and prevention/treatment resources exist.
  • Warning signs of a mental health crisis (including suicide/self-harm) can be recognized, and there are known ways to seek help for yourself or others; stigma around mental health can be actively reduced.
  • Physical fitness has multiple components; CPR/AED and basic emergency response are learnable, teachable skills.
  • Digital communication and social media carry safety, consent, and boundary implications; school-safety practices exist for emergencies.
  • Substances (alcohol, tobacco, nicotine, cannabis, and others) carry physical, mental, and legal consequences; substance-use disorder, overdose, and recovery are real, addressable situations, not just cautionary abstractions.
  • Health-related decisions and goals can be analyzed, planned, and evaluated using a structured process, not just instinct.

docs.title: Food and Nutrition
docs.text:
• Designing a nutrition plan that meets personal needs and preferences (9.1.1.1)
  • Using food labels to analyze nutrient values and their health impact (9.1.1.2)
  • Evaluating personal beverage choices using hydration/sugar/caffeine evidence (9.1.1.3)
  • Evaluating meals/snacks for daily life and physical activity using nutrition strategies (9.1.1.4)
  • How cultural traditions, community initiatives, and food systems affect healthy diets and chronic-disease risk (9.1.1.5)

docs.title: Human Growth and Development and Sexual Health
docs.text:
• Characteristics of healthy relationships and handling conflict/pressure (9.2.1.1)
  • How cultural, social, historical, and personal factors shape relationship structures (9.2.1.2)
  • Showing dignity and compassion for all people across situations and relationships (9.2.1.3)
  • How guidance from family, trusted adults, and culturally safe healthcare providers influences health/relationship decisions (9.2.1.4)
  • Adolescents' rights to access healthcare services; what to expect from youth-friendly providers (9.2.1.5)
  • How stereotypes, bias, myths, stigma, and prejudice affect relationships, behavior, health, and access to culturally safe healthcare (9.2.1.6)
  • STI prevention, treatment, and health outcomes, using culturally safe and respectful approaches (9.2.1.7)
  • The role of healthcare services and community-based programs in supporting healthy relationships/sexual health, and how culturally responsive services reduce barriers (9.2.1.8)
  • Setting/communicating personal boundaries to support decision-making that prevents pregnancy and STIs, reflecting mutual respect (9.2.1.9)

docs.title: Mental and Emotional Health
docs.text:
• Deciding when/how to seek help for mental/emotional health concerns, including thoughts of suicide or self-harm (9.3.1.1)
  • Causes, symptoms, and effects of depression and anxiety; treatment options (9.3.1.2)
  • Evaluating mental health challenges and peer crises; supporting others while maintaining boundaries (9.3.1.3)
  • How empathy and communication foster healthy relationships and nonviolent conflict resolution, including Indigenous restorative-justice approaches (9.3.1.4)
  • Strategies for managing emotions and supporting intra/interpersonal wellbeing, drawing on cultural teachings (9.3.1.5)
  • Designing strategies to foster a supportive, inclusive environment that addresses exclusion, bullying, stereotyping, prejudice, discrimination (9.3.1.6)
  • Reducing stigma and increasing mental health awareness in schools and communities (9.3.1.7)
  • Strategies to maintain brain health; Alzheimer's disease and other dementias; supporting an elder with cognitive impairment (9.3.1.8)

docs.title: Personal Health and Wellness
docs.text:
• How personal care practices (sleep, rest) influence lifelong health, and how culture/community/social conditions create health disparities (9.4.1.1)
  • How access to physical activity differs across communities; safe participation practices; systemic inequities in health opportunity (9.4.1.2)
  • Demonstrating CPR techniques and knowing when/how to use an AED (9.4.1.3)
  • How behavioral, environmental, and lifestyle factors influence infectious and chronic disease, and strategies to prevent them (9.4.1.4)

docs.title: Personal Safety and Violence Prevention
docs.text:
• How digital content, social media, and online communication affect expectations, behaviors, and boundaries (9.5.1.1)
  • Safe/appropriate actions for threats, harmful content, or online emergencies (9.5.1.2)
  • Evaluating school safety practices/policies, including school shootings (9.5.1.3)
  • Communicating, interpreting, and withdrawing consent; how power dynamics and law (federal, state, local, tribal) affect consent (9.5.1.4)

docs.title: Substance Use Awareness and Prevention
docs.text:
• How substance use affects mental health, brain function, and physiology, and disrupts relationships/school/work, considering Indigenous views of health (9.6.1.1)
  • How substance use affects decision-making; coping strategies/alternatives drawing on cultural practices (9.6.1.2)
  • Differences between commercial tobacco addiction and traditional tobacco/plant medicine use (9.6.1.3)
  • Risks of mixing medications/substances; safe actions vs. traditional medicine use (9.6.1.4)
  • Supporting yourself/others in preventing or reducing substance use, including cultural resilience strategies (9.6.1.5)
  • Short- and long-term physical, mental, and relational effects of alcohol, tobacco, nicotine, cannabis, and other substances (9.6.1.6)
  • Recognizing overdose signs and appropriate emergency response (9.6.1.7)
  • How communities integrate cultural practices with prevention/treatment for resilience and recovery (9.6.1.8)
  • Community laws, policies, and financial/social costs of substance use, including tribal sovereignty in lawmaking (9.6.1.9)
  • How policy/regulation shapes marketing and availability of alcohol, tobacco, and other substances, and resulting health disparities (9.6.1.10)

docs.text:
• Analyzing how public health policy, law, and school/community environments influence health practices (9.7.2.1)
  • Analyzing how culture, peers, norms, attitudes, and beliefs influence health practices (9.7.2.2)
  • Evaluating how individual, interpersonal, community, societal, and environmental factors influence health practices (9.7.2.3)
  • Analyzing the accessibility/validity of trusted adults, professionals, and health resources (9.7.3.1)
  • Using and evaluating the validity/reliability/accessibility of health information, products, and services (9.7.3.2)
  • Analyzing verbal/nonverbal communication across communication types (9.7.4.1)
  • Analyzing conflict-resolution and negotiation skills (9.7.4.2)
  • Evaluating communication related to boundaries and consent (9.7.4.3)
  • Evaluating refusal skills/strategies (9.7.4.4)
  • Analyzing how health decisions affect personal/community wellbeing from multiple perspectives (9.7.5.1)
  • Analyzing options and consequences in health-related decisions (9.7.5.2)
  • Choosing and justifying the healthiest option; evaluating outcomes (9.7.5.3)
  • Evaluating personal health/wellbeing factors to justify goal-setting focus areas (9.7.6.1)
  • Using an individual, supported, or collaborative goal-setting process (9.7.6.2)
  • Formulating strategies to support a personal health goal; evaluating the process/outcomes (9.7.6.3)
  • Evaluating supports/barriers to health-related practices (9.7.7.1)
  • Adapting and demonstrating practices/behaviors; evaluating their impact (9.7.7.2)
  • Examining factors affecting health promotion at individual through environmental levels (9.7.8.1)
  • Formulating/justifying a fact-supported health message for varied audiences (9.7.8.2)
  • Evaluating and refining the process/outcomes/effectiveness of health promotion efforts (9.7.8.3)

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text: Outcomes below are grouped by Bloom's Taxonomy level and traced to their source benchmark codes. Grade 9-12 is heavily weighted toward Evaluate — the standards repeatedly use "apply skill cues to evaluate" language at this terminal band, reflecting career/college/community readiness.

docs.title: 1. Remember
docs.text:
By the end of Grade 12, the student will be able to:

  1. Identify safe and appropriate actions to take in response to online threats, harmful content, or emergencies (9.5.1.2).
  2. Recognize the signs of an overdose from medications or substances (9.6.1.7).

docs.title: 2. Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain the characteristics of healthy relationships and how to handle challenges, including conflict or pressure (9.2.1.1).
  2. Describe how to show dignity and compassion for all people in a range of situations and relationships (9.2.1.3).
  3. Identify what to expect from youth-friendly healthcare providers (9.2.1.5).
  4. Summarize STI prevention, treatment, and health outcomes using culturally safe and respectful approaches (9.2.1.7).
  5. Explain strategies to maintain brain health and describe Alzheimer's disease and other dementias (9.3.1.8).
  6. Summarize the short- and long-term physical, mental, and relational effects of alcohol, commercial tobacco, nicotine, cannabis, and other substances (9.6.1.6).
  7. Explain appropriate responses to a suspected overdose, including contacting emergency services (9.6.1.7).

docs.title: 3. Apply
docs.text:
1. Demonstrate how to support others through a mental health challenge or peer crisis while maintaining boundaries (9.3.1.3).
  2. Demonstrate safe participation in physical activity, including proper equipment use, warm-up/cool-down routines, and hydration (9.4.1.2).
  3. Demonstrate CPR techniques and know when and how to use an AED (9.4.1.3).
  4. Apply safe and appropriate actions in response to online threats or emergencies (9.5.1.2).
  5. Use an individual, supported, or collaborative goal-setting process as appropriate (9.7.6.2).
  6. Adapt and demonstrate a variety of practices and behaviors that support health and wellbeing (9.7.7.2).

  4. Examine adolescents' rights to access a range of healthcare services (9.2.1.5).
  5. Analyze how stereotypes, bias, myths, stigma, and prejudice affect relationships, behaviors, and health (9.2.1.6).
  6. Analyze how setting and communicating personal boundaries supports decisions that prevent pregnancy and STIs (9.2.1.9).
  7. Analyze how empathy and communication foster healthy relationships and nonviolent conflict resolution (9.3.1.4).
  8. Analyze how access to physical activity differs across communities (9.4.1.2).
  9. Analyze how substance use can affect decision-making (9.6.1.2).
  10. Analyze ways to support yourself and others in preventing or reducing substance use (9.6.1.5).
  11. Analyze how policies and regulations shape the marketing and availability of alcohol, tobacco, and other substances (9.6.1.10).
  12. Analyze how public health policies, laws, and community/school environments influence health practices (9.7.2.1).
  13. Analyze how culture, peers, perceived norms, attitudes, and beliefs influence health practices (9.7.2.2).
  14. Analyze the accessibility and validity of trusted adults, health professionals, and other resources (9.7.3.1).
  15. Analyze verbal and nonverbal communication skills across various types of communication (9.7.4.1).
  16. Analyze conflict-resolution and negotiation skills for a variety of health-related situations (9.7.4.2).
  17. Analyze how health-related decisions may affect personal and community wellbeing from a variety of perspectives (9.7.5.1).
  18. Analyze a variety of options and potential consequences when making health-related decisions (9.7.5.2).
  19. Examine factors affecting health promotion at individual through environmental levels (9.7.8.1).

docs.title: 5. Evaluate
docs.text:
1. Evaluate personal beverage choices using evidence about hydration, sugar, and caffeine content (9.1.1.3).
  2. Evaluate meals and snacks for daily life and physical activity using nutrition strategies (9.1.1.4).
  3. Evaluate how guidance from family, trusted adults, and culturally safe healthcare providers can influence health/relationship decisions (9.2.1.4).
  4. Evaluate the role of healthcare services and community-based programs in supporting healthy relationships and sexual health (9.2.1.8).
  5. Evaluate situations to decide when and how to seek help for mental or emotional health concerns, including thoughts of suicide or self-harm (9.3.1.1).
  6. Analyze the causes, symptoms, and effects of depression and anxiety, and evaluate strategies and treatment options (9.3.1.2).
  7. Evaluate mental health challenges and peer crises (9.3.1.3).
  8. Evaluate strategies for managing emotions and their support for intrapersonal and interpersonal wellbeing (9.3.1.5).
  9. Evaluate and develop strategies that reduce stigma and increase awareness of mental health in schools and communities (9.3.1.7).
  10. Evaluate how personal care practices, including sleep and rest, influence lifelong health (9.4.1.1).
  11. Evaluate how behavioral, environmental, and lifestyle factors influence infectious and chronic diseases, and assess prevention strategies (9.4.1.4).
  12. Evaluate how digital content, social media, and online communication affect expectations, behaviors, and boundaries (9.5.1.1).
  13. Evaluate school safety practices and policies related to emergencies, including school shootings (9.5.1.3).
  14. Evaluate how to communicate, interpret, and withdraw consent, and how power dynamics and law affect consent (9.5.1.4).
  15. Evaluate how substance use affects mental health, brain function, and overall physiological health (9.6.1.1).
  16. Evaluate the differences between commercial tobacco addiction and the traditional use of tobacco and other plant medicines (9.6.1.3).
  17. Evaluate strategies to prevent harmful interactions when mixing medications and other substances (9.6.1.4).
  18. Evaluate how various communities integrate cultural practices with prevention and treatment approaches (9.6.1.8).

  21. Evaluate how individual, interpersonal, community, societal, and environmental factors influence health practices (9.7.2.3).
  22. Use and evaluate the validity, reliability, and accessibility of health information, products, services, and other resources (9.7.3.2).
  23. Evaluate communication related to boundaries and expressing or withdrawing consent (9.7.4.3).
  24. Evaluate refusal skills and strategies in a variety of health-related situations (9.7.4.4).
  25. Choose the healthiest option, justify why it's the healthiest choice, and evaluate outcomes (9.7.5.3).
  26. Evaluate personal health, wellbeing, and factors to justify focus areas for goal setting (9.7.6.1).
  27. Evaluate supports and barriers to engaging in health-related practices (9.7.7.1).
  28. Evaluate and explain the impact of practices and behaviors that support health and wellbeing (9.7.7.2).
  29. Evaluate and refine the process, outcomes, and overall effectiveness of promoting health, safety, and wellbeing (9.7.8.3).

docs.title: 6. Create
docs.text:
1. Design a nutrition plan that meets personal needs and preferences (9.1.1.1).
  2. Design and evaluate strategies to foster a supportive and inclusive environment that addresses exclusion, bullying, and discrimination (9.3.1.6).
  3. Develop coping strategies or healthy alternatives when substance use affects decision-making, drawing on culturally grounded practices (9.6.1.2).
  4. Formulate strategies to support achieving a personal health goal (9.7.6.3).
  5. Formulate and justify a health-enhancing position or message about an issue, supported by facts and tailored to a variety of audiences (9.7.8.2).

docs.title: How to Use This Textbook
docs.text: This band contains 15 chapters that build on each other in order — each chapter assumes the concepts introduced in earlier chapters, so it works best read start to finish on a first pass. Every chapter opens with a short summary and a numbered list of the concepts it covers, drawn directly from the Grade 9-12 learning graph, so you can see exactly what you are expected to know before and after reading it. Students entering this band without an earlier one should first review the bridging concepts in the course description. Teachers can use the concept lists and prerequisite links to plan units, identify review points, or jump directly to the material a lesson needs.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text:
1. Food and Nutrition — Students design a personal nutrition plan and evaluate food labels, beverages, meals, and snacks, then examine how culture, community initiatives, and food systems shape chronic-disease risk.
  2. Relationships and Respect — Students examine how relationship structures form and vary, what makes a relationship healthy, how to handle conflict and pressure, and how empathy and cultural context shape relationships.
  3. Consent and Boundaries — Students build a working model of consent and personal boundaries, including how to communicate, interpret, and withdraw consent, and how power and law affect it.
  4. Healthcare Access and Sexual Health — Students learn to access culturally safe, youth-friendly healthcare, understand STI prevention and treatment, and evaluate community sexual-health programs and boundary-based prevention.
  5. Mental Health and Crisis Support — Students learn when and how to seek help for depression, anxiety, or suicide/self-harm risk, how to support a peer in crisis while maintaining boundaries, and how to reduce mental health stigma.
  6. Conflict Resolution and Inclusion — Students develop nonviolent conflict-resolution and emotion-management skills, drawing on cultural teachings and restorative-justice approaches, and design strategies for inclusive, bullying-free environments.
  7. Brain Health, Sleep, and Emergency Care — Students learn habits that protect brain health across the lifespan, including support for elders with dementia, the role of sleep in wellbeing, and how to perform CPR and use an AED.
  8. Health Equity and Disease Prevention — Students analyze how social conditions create health disparities and inequitable access to physical activity, then evaluate strategies to prevent chronic and infectious disease.
  9. Digital and School Safety — Students evaluate how digital content and social media affect relationships and boundaries, how to respond to online threats, and how to assess school safety practices and emergency preparedness.
  10. Substances: Effects and Safer Choices — Students analyze how substance use affects the brain, body, decision-making, and relationships, compare commercial and traditional tobacco use, and learn safe medication practices and coping strategies.
  11. Substance Recovery and Resilience — Students examine the short- and long-term effects of specific substances, learn to recognize and respond to overdose, and explore culturally grounded paths to treatment, recovery, and resilience.
  12. Substance Policy and Law — Students evaluate community laws, financial and social costs, tribal sovereignty, and marketing policy related to substance use and the disparities these policies create.
  13. Influences on Health Behavior — Students analyze how policy, culture, peers, norms, and community conditions shape health practices, and evaluate the reliability of health information, communication, and refusal skills.
  14. Health Decision-Making and Goal-Setting — Students apply a structured process to weigh options and consequences, choose and justify the healthiest choice, and set and pursue personal health goals individually or collaboratively.
  15. Health Promotion and Behavior Change — Students evaluate supports and barriers to healthy behavior, adapt their own practices, and design and refine fact-based health messages for different audiences.

docs.title: Learning Graph — Grade 9-12
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for the Grade 9-12 band of the Health Education intelligent textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this band. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the band. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

This band's graph is the largest in the series — 136 concepts, slightly larger than Grade 6-8's 133 — because Grade 9-12 is the terminal band and enumerates the largest topic set of any band (61 topic benchmarks plus 20 Skill Standards benchmarks, see the Course Description Assessment for the rationale). It builds directly on the Grade 6-8 band's graph across all six strands, extending each toward the evaluative, systemic, and cultural reasoning that defines this band: designing and evaluating personal plans, analyzing policy and systemic factors, and reasoning about cultural safety, Indigenous perspectives, and tribal sovereignty.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this band. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy — Grade 9-12
docs.text:
This band uses the same eight-category scheme established at Grade 6-8. The Human Growth and Development category remains GROW (Human Growth, Development, and Sexual Health), and Substance Use Awareness and Prevention (SUB) continues as its own category. Skill Standards (SKIL) remains a single category because, at 37 of 136 concepts (27.2%), it stays under the 30% balance ceiling, even though its raw benchmark count (20) is the largest Skill Standards set in the series so far and this band's Skill Standards benchmarks are unusually dense (most are single-sentence "Analyze/Evaluate X" statements that still expand to 1-2 concepts each rather than the 2-3 sub-concepts typical of Grade 6-8's compound benchmarks).

Category TaxonomyID Description Foundations FOUND Bridging/anchor concept carried forward from earlier bands that connects concepts across strands ("Health"). Food and Nutrition FOOD Personal nutrition planning, food label and nutrient analysis, beverage evaluation, meal/snack evaluation, cultural food traditions, and food systems/chronic-disease-risk/community initiatives. Human Growth, Development, and Sexual Health GROW Relationship structures and characteristics, cultural/historical influences on relationships, dignity and compassion, culturally safe healthcare access, STI prevention/treatment, community-based sexual health programs, boundaries, and consent. Mental and Emotional Health EMOT Suicide/self-harm help-seeking, depression and anxiety, supporting peers in crisis, empathy and conflict resolution, Indigenous restorative justice, emotion management, inclusive-environment design, stigma reduction, and brain health/dementia. Personal Health and Wellness WELL Sleep and rest, health disparities and systemic inequity, physical activity access and safety, CPR/AED, and behavioral/environmental factors in disease risk and prevention. Personal Safety and Violence Prevention SAFE Digital content and social media effects on relationships/boundaries, online threat and emergency response, school safety practices, and consent communication/withdrawal/power dynamics/law. Substance Use Awareness and Prevention SUB Effects of substance use on mental health, brain function, physiology, relationships, school/work, and decision-making; coping strategies; tobacco/medication safety; overdose recognition and response; substance use disorder treatment and recovery; and substance-related law, policy, and health disparities. Skill Standards SKIL Cross-cutting skills: influences on health practices, evaluating trusted adults and health information, communication and negotiation, refusal skills, health decision-making, goal-setting, adapting health behaviors, and health message design/promotion.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Grade 9-12 course description is the largest and most cognitively demanding document in the series. It is derived from the 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards and enumerates 61 benchmark-coded topics across six content strands (Food and Nutrition; Human Growth, Development, and Sexual Health; Mental and Emotional Health; Personal Health and Wellness; Personal Safety and Violence Prevention; Substance Use Awareness and Prevention) plus a large cross-cutting Skill Standards group (20 benchmarks). This slightly exceeds Grade 6-8's 59 topic benchmarks + 19 Skill Standards benchmarks (78 total), and is the terminal band, culminating in career/college/community readiness framing.

This assessment evaluates the description against a right-sized concept target of approximately 130-145 concepts (not the skill's generic 200-concept default), consistent with the proportional scaling applied to Grade 6-8 (120-135 concepts) and reflecting a modest increase in raw benchmark count plus this band's markedly higher density of compound, multi-clause benchmarks.
